Abstract

This portfolio is a record of my journey toward becoming a Master Guide, the highest level of leadership training offered within Adventurer and Pathfinder ministry. It follows the same four-part shape Luke used to describe the growth of Christ Himself: wisdom, stature, and favor with both God and man. Over the course of this program I am not simply collecting honors and signatures — I am being formed as a leader who can teach, mentor, and shepherd young people the way I have been shepherded. Each section of this portfolio mirrors a section of the official curriculum: the prerequisites that open the door, the leadership training that shapes how I think, the physical and outdoor disciplines that shape how I live, the spiritual disciplines that shape how I walk with God, and the community work that shapes how I serve others. As I complete each requirement it is recorded here with its supporting evidence, so that by the time I stand for investiture, this stands as a true account of the road I walked to get there.

About

Muwulya Jesse Mwebaza

I worship at SDA Church Makerere, in the Central Kampala Zone of the Central Uganda Conference, under the Uganda Union. My journey in Pathfinder ministry began long before I ever heard the term “Master Guide” — it started with a love for the outdoors, for badges earned around a campfire, and for the quiet example of the staff members who gave up their Sabbath afternoons to invest in us as young people. Over time that love grew into a conviction: this ministry had shaped me, and I wanted to help shape others the same way. Pursuing the Master Guide award is my way of stepping fully into that calling — sharpening my leadership, deepening my walk with God, and preparing to serve my club, my zone, and my conference with a steadier hand and a fuller heart.

Before you begin

Prerequisites

The five entry requirements every candidate must meet before starting the Master Guide curriculum.

0%
Section summary

Before the journey begins

The prerequisites are not warm-up exercises. The manual requires all of them to be finished before the programme proper starts, and the three-year completion window only begins once they are done. Their common theme is trustworthiness: the church is establishing that you are a committed member, that you are legally able to carry adult responsibility, that children are safe with you, that you have thought about why you want this, and that you have the basic competence to run club ministry.

Notice how much of this is about other people rather than about you. Baptism ties you to a congregation. The background check protects minors. The mentor conversation puts an experienced leader alongside you. Even the workshops are about serving a club well.

What this section develops

  • Why the church treats youth leadership as a position of trust rather than a reward for enthusiasm.
  • The moral and civil duty of child protection, and what safeguarding looks like in practice.
  • How to organise a club, plan a programme, run ceremonies, and teach a class.
  • That prayer and counsel come before major decisions, not after them.

As masterguides we ought to take on the role of a shepherd to the youth and that means we need to protect children both at church and away from church.

When enrolling for teaching, due to diligence the following must be done

  • People who teach but are not MGs are volunteers and basic staff training is done for them.
  • Background check should be done
  • Church discipline is strictly managed
  • Gate keeping should be done to stop predators at the door.

  • Do not allow distraction keep watch of the children.
  • Places with many rooms should be limited of access.
  • Never be alone with a child.
  • Criminal background checks should be done.
  • Willingness to stand up to abuse.
  • Never ignore child abuse.

    Master Guide Class 2 — Makerere
    By MG. Emmanuel R. Ssemwogerere

    Introduction to teaching

    • Concepts
    • Achievement
    • Responsibility
    • Respect

    Achievement
    There should be a sense of purpose.
    Learners need to achieve what is expected of them.
    Encourage personal growth, skills development & goal setting.
    Teach and reach, physical, mental & spiritual milestones.
    Activities should include progressive learning, challenges (that's how pathfinders/adventurers learn).
    You should motivate learners and recognise their achievements.

    Responsibility
    Young people should learn to accept & faithfully carry on responsibilities assigned to them. Same applies to teachers. These responsibilities should be given according to age and experience.
    Instil success for accountability of actions, tasks.
    Help them develop leadership skills and a strong work ethic.
    Activities done should promote teamwork but also personal initiatives.
    Model students' behaviors & also skill them to take ownership of their conduct.

    • Respect
    • Need to learn & respect the principles of authority.
    • Teachers' discipline & obedience is equally important.
    • Teachers should create rules & regulations for the class.
    • Make them understand the value of structure.
    • Activities should include mentorship, role models.
    • Teachers should demonstrate kindness and fairness.

    Effective teaching requires use of teaching that enables different learning styles. Learners have different ways of capturing material.

    Learning styles and their characteristics

    1. Visual learners.

    • They prefer viewing or seeing info.
    • Tend to remember info through images, diagrams, charts etc.
    • Often enjoy visual aid.
    • Have a good photographic memory.
    • Good at recalling faces, location, places etc.
    • Benefit from reading & demonstration.

    2. Auditory
    Best learn through listening.
    Prefer lectures, discussions rather than hands on.
    Find it helps reading loudly.
    Tend to excel in environments where verbal communication is key, e.g. debates, discussions.

    • Tactile or Kinetic
    • Learn through hands-on experience.
    • Prefer to engage in activities like role playing.
    • May struggle with passive learning.
    • Struggle with long periods of seating.
    • Tend to learn through trial & error and enjoy interactive practical tasks.

Section I

Leadership Identity & Growth (Wisdom)

Developing the inner conviction, knowledge, and skill that shape a Christian leader.

0%
Section summary

Leadership identity and growth

Wisdom in the Luke 2:52 model is the mental dimension — but the manual is not asking for information alone. This section pairs eight training workshops with two books, two self-assessments, and a full year of actual staff service. That combination is deliberate: theory is introduced in a workshop, tested against Scripture and Ellen White, checked against your own gifts and temperament, and then proved in front of real children who will not pretend a badly planned programme was good.

The recurring idea across the material already in your file is that Christian authority is exercised as service. Leadership is described as a gift exercised with the attitude of a servant, and discipline is framed as restoration rather than punishment.

What this section develops

  • That true education develops the whole person — mind, character and hands — with God as the source of wisdom.
  • How to identify your own spiritual gifts, and why the body of Christ needs gifts unlike your own.
  • How temperament and personality shape the way you lead, and where your natural weaknesses lie.
  • That a year of staff service, with 75% attendance and honors actually taught, is what converts training into competence.

    Workshop notes distinguishing vision from mission, plus the church's and youth ministry's mission statements and objectives.

    Read full document

    VISION AND MISSION

    Vision — the long-term desire of what you want your life to look like, or want your life to be.
    Mission — why you're created.
    Both vision and mission co-exist. The mission statement is the compass that points to the vision, and the mission has objectives to help us keep on track.

    Things to look to when setting mission and vision

    • Keep them clear.
    • Simple, short, precise.
    • In an understandable language.
    • Use short statements instead of ambiguity.

    Characteristics one has to have to set up mission and vision

    • Be of sound mind.
    • Know the intention of youth ministry.

    a) Vision and mission as a personal objective — why it is important

    • Essential for providing clear direction.
    • Uniqueness of human beings.
    • Purpose for living.
    • Motivates us in whatever we do.
    • Helps us build resilience in whatever we do or try to do.
    • Helps us foster our personal growth.
    • Mission drives your daily actions (the values of how to get to our vision).

    b) Mission and vision of our church

    Vision: looks at the remnant church.
    Mission: to make disciples of Jesus Christ, preaching the everlasting gospel.

    Our responsibility (Total Member Involvement)

    • Grounded in the Bible.
    • Proclaim the three angels' message.
    • Disciple people.
    • Prepare everyone for the second coming (Revelation 14:12).
    • NB: Our leaders get packaged information and give it to us to act as a guide to fulfil our responsibility.

    c) Mission and vision of the youth ministry

    • To lead young people into a saving life and a lifelong relationship with Jesus Christ.
    • Preaching the gospel in this generation.
    • Being involved all the time.
    • The relationship is a gradual process; it grows daily.

    Objectives

    • To save and guide the youth.
    • Be mission focused to spread the Advent message.

    Important themes and goals in youth ministry

    • Salvation.
    • Inclusivity and diversity in all programs and messages, regardless of age, race, etc.
    • Empowerment — using their talents for God through leadership and ministry.
    • The love of God compels us.

    Key benefits of having a vision- and mission-driven life

    • Direction and focus.
    • Setting up a purpose for your life.
    • Keeps us motivated in what we do.
    • Keeps us committed to our goals and what we intend to achieve.
    • Increases our resilience.
    • Helps us overcome obstacles and stay on track.
    • Being accountable.
    • Helps enhance self-awareness.

    Things to avoid as we make vision and mission

    • Do not be too generic.
    • Avoid not being clear.
    • Avoid not being specific with what you want.
    • Avoid using complicated language; it should be easy to remember.
    • Avoid confusing mission with vision.
  • Christian Leadership
    Evidence on file Christian Leadership Summary.docx

    Summary on love, modesty, self-development, discipline, and vision as pillars of Christian leadership.

    Read full document

    CHRISTIAN LEADERSHIP

    Christian leadership is the act of guiding and directing a group of people, guided by divine guidance and started in the garden of Eden when Adam and Eve were given authority over other creatures. Effective Christian leaders demonstrate love, humility, and integrity, and prioritize spiritual growth and development. It involves influencing others out of Christ's interests to accomplish God's purpose for and through them.

    A human being is made up of three domains: cognitive, psychomotor, and affective. Basic goals of psychology include understanding, predicting, describing, influencing, and improving the quality of life.

    The principles of Christian leadership include love, modesty, self-development, motivational, correction, integrity, following God's will, and commitment. Love is essential for understanding others, respecting their concerns, believing in their gifts, supporting their dreams, and challenging their flaws. Modesty is important for Christians to avoid arrogance and not be proud of their abilities. Self-development is a long-term process for Christians, but leaders should make more time to seek God and develop spiritually.

    Christian leaders should also have a clear mission, vision, and motivation, and be able to communicate effectively and make informed decisions. Additionally, leaders should be able to delegate tasks, solve problems, and manage risks. Effective management involves planning, organizing, directing, and controlling resources.

    Discipline is also essential in leadership, and involves setting rules and regulations to enforce obedience and moral behavior. Leaders should understand the different forms of discipline, including preventive, supportive, and corrective discipline, and apply them appropriately.

    In conclusion, Christian leadership involves understanding, guiding, and directing others out of Christ's interests, focusing on love, modesty, self-development, motivation, correction, integrity, following God's will, and commitment.

  • Discipline & Discipleship
    Evidence on file Discipline and Discipleship.pdf

    Church discipline grounded in Matthew 18, its reasons and processes, and what discipleship means as a growth process.

    Read full document

    DISCIPLINE AND DISCIPLESHIP

    Discipline
    It is all based on the Bible, and it is carried out by the church business meeting.

    Code of behaviour
    Church discipline has been present over the years. It is witnessed in the story of Korah, Miriam, and Aaron, who were punished when they disobeyed Moses. We learn that discipline has guidelines in Matthew 18:15. God's first priority after a wrongdoing is reconciliation, and the Bible encourages us to be calm and avoid angry words and scuffles.

    No officer or committee has jurisdiction to discard a member without following the steps stipulated in the Bible. However, if all the steps are followed and there is no change, then sin is called out and prevented from spreading by taking disciplinary action. The purity and health of the church must be preserved at all costs — "for everything locked on earth is locked in heaven."

    No one is allowed to make independent decisions apart from the church, especially on matters concerning the church. The church was created in a way that it doesn't rely on one person; no human being has the ultimate power. God holds the church as a body, and therefore leaders must ensure the purity of the church — if they allow impurity, those sins are on them.

    If church discipline were not in place, the entire church would have been fragmented. Discipline safeguards unity. Christians should avoid tendencies that divide them, and those who refuse to work in unity dishonour God. God's order and unity are embodied in the Holy Trinity. Members who express selfishness and impatience with the church's recommendations should also be put on discipline.

    Why church discipline?

    To safeguard the church's image and to uphold the faith of believers.

    Reasons for church discipline

    • Denial of faith in the fundamentals of the gospel and beliefs, and teaching contrary to them.
    • Dishonoring the commandments of God.
    • Dishonoring the doctrine of marriage — fornication, homosexuality, incest, bestiality, production of pornography, remarrying a divorced person.
    • Physical violence.
    • Fraud, wrongful representation of the church.
    • Disorderly behaviour that brings reproach to the church.
    • Persistent disregard of church authority.
    • Drug abuse and dealing drugs.
    • Unlawful business.
    • Treachery.

    The process of church discipline

    • Discipline by vote of censure — a way for the church to disagree or disapprove of the actions of the member in question. It is also done to impress upon a member to turn from their ways by giving them a probation, given for a maximum of 12 months, after which it is relieved, extended, or the member is removed from church books.
    • Discipline by vote of removal of a member from church books — this is rare and is the most extreme measure of discipline; therefore, all other processes of church discipline must first fail for this action to be taken. A member cannot be discarded for petty reasons; the reason must be major.

    Reasons for discipline by removal from church books

    • Death.
    • Contradictory teachings.
    • Violation of the Sabbath.
    • Disregarding the church's effort to correct them.
    • Public offences.
    • Witchcraft.
    • Actions that obstruct ministry.
    • Legal representation in church discipline.

    The rest is to be found in the Church Manual, chapter 8. It is crucial and paramount for every member to have a Church Manual.

    Discipleship
    It was the first name given to Christ's followers before the word "Christians."
    Disciple and discipleship are different; Ephesians 4:11 and John 8:31 describe who a disciple is, and Matthew 28:19-20 is the greatest mission of the church.
    Discipleship is a process and set of practices by which one can grow their spiritual life.

  • Child & Youth Evangelism
    Evidence on file Child & Youth Evangelism Summary.docx

    Notes on reaching children through relationship, storytelling, and age-appropriate methods.

    Read full document

    CHILD AND YOUTH EVANGELISM

    Child evangelism aims to lead children to Jesus, recognizing their importance as the future of the Church. However, contemporary cultural changes present challenges, as today's children are accustomed to fast-paced lifestyles and are adept with technology. This necessitates a thoughtful approach to evangelism that considers understanding children's unique emotional, social, physical, spiritual, and mental needs using engaging methods, and building relationships, individuals which makes a positive impact on children's spiritual lives.

    Effective child evangelism involves building relationships and trust with children, using engaging methods like storytelling, games, and activities to share the gospel. Bible stories and lessons can teach children about God's love and principles, encouraging them to make informed decisions about their faith. Training volunteers and staff to work with children is essential, as is developing age-specific programs and materials.

    Involving parents and caregivers in child evangelism efforts is also vital, as they play a significant role in supporting children's spiritual growth and development. Child Evangelism aims to empower individuals to share the gospel with children in a way that is both engaging and meaningful. By understanding child development and using effective strategies, individuals can make a positive impact on children's spiritual lives.

    Ultimately, the goal of child evangelism is to foster a love for Jesus Christ and His teachings in children. By equipping individuals with the skills and knowledge necessary to share the gospel with children, the syllabus can help support children's spiritual growth and development.

    Evidence on file Temperaments & Personalities — Summary Notes.pdf

    The four classic temperaments with biblical examples, strengths, weaknesses, and growth needs for each.

    Read full document

    TEMPERAMENTS & PERSONALITIES — SUMMARY NOTES

    Introduction
    Temperament is the combination of characteristics and qualities that form an individual's distinctive personality. It refers to how we naturally react to people, situations, and the world around us. Some individuals respond quickly, others take time to analyze; some are more emotional, cautious, or driven than others. Understanding these differences helps us live harmoniously and serve more effectively.
    "Man is a social being — learning to live among others requires understanding ourselves first."

    Why study temperaments?

    • To understand ourselves and others better.
    • To improve relationships, teamwork, and spiritual growth.
    • To accept and appreciate our differences rather than criticize.
    • To increase self-awareness and identify personal strengths and weaknesses.
    • To manage stress and reactions by recognizing the pressures we face.
    • To realize that no temperament is perfect — each has strengths and weaknesses.
    • To practice tolerance, patience, and love as God's children.

    Romans 3:23 — "For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." We are all sinners saved by grace, each designed differently for a purpose.

    Note: Most people are a blend of temperaments — one dominant (primary) and one supporting (secondary).

    THE FOUR CLASSIC TEMPERAMENTS

    • Melancholy — The Thinker
    • Choleric — The Leader
    • Sanguine — The Talker
    • Phlegmatic — The Peacemaker
    • Each temperament is unique, with its own set of strengths, weaknesses, and growth needs.

    1. Melancholy (Analytical, Wise, and Quiet) — "Abakuyege," The Thinkers
    Biblical example: Moses.
    - Deep thinker, cautious, and careful in decisions.
    - Sometimes slow to act (gave excuses to God).
    - Compassionate intercessor — stood in the gap for Israel.
    - Yet struggled with anger (killed an Egyptian, broke the tablets, struck the rock twice).
    Strengths: thorough, organized, and dependable; loyal, disciplined, and self-sacrificing; compassionate and analytical; high standards, loving perfection and truth; values time and punctuality; loves tradition and order.
    Weaknesses: perfectionist and overly critical; sensitive and easily hurt; tends to overthink or replay mistakes; moody and easily discouraged; quick-tempered under pressure.
    Needs to learn: to be realistic, not overly idealistic; to accept that no one is perfect; to forgive themselves and others easily.

    2. Choleric (Strong-Willed, Active, and Decisive) — "Bawologoma," The Lions / Workers
    Biblical example: Paul (Saul).
    - Determined, visionary, and fearless in mission.
    - Brought great change, wrote letters, and served tirelessly.
    - Led others boldly but sometimes harshly.
    Strengths: natural-born leaders and visionaries; goal-oriented and decisive; independent, confident, and productive; motivates others to act and take responsibility; faces challenges head-on; strong-willed, courageous, and action-driven; excellent organizers, planners, and achievers.
    Weaknesses: bossy and domineering; argumentative and impatient; often insensitive to others' emotions; prone to anger or shouting; doesn't like being controlled or corrected; can be manipulative or coercive.
    Needs to learn: patience and gentleness; to be more loving and compassionate; to listen and involve others in decisions; to recognize that success requires humility.

    3. Sanguine (Cheerful, Talkative, and Sociable) — "Enkyima / Engonge," The Fun-Lovers / Talkers
    Biblical example: Peter.
    - Energetic and outgoing — left everything to follow Jesus.
    - Quick to speak and promise, but often acted impulsively.
    - Loved Jesus deeply and was later transformed into a faithful leader.
    Strengths: warm, friendly, and inspiring; encouraging and generous; loves people and brings joy to others; expressive, entertaining, and full of life; great communicator and storyteller; good at motivating and comforting others; hospitable and compassionate.
    Weaknesses: disorganized and forgetful; makes promises they may not keep; easily distracted or emotional; impulsive and talkative, and may dominate conversations; struggles with consistency and follow-through; can be restless or self-centered.
    Needs to learn: discipline, focus, and purposefulness; to balance fun with responsibility; to take commitments seriously; that God values maturity as much as enthusiasm.
    "Jesus restored Peter, proving that God transforms even the impulsive into dependable leaders."

    4. Phlegmatic (Calm, Loyal, and Peaceful) — "Battugga," The Peacemakers / Observers
    Biblical example: Abraham.
    - Peace-loving and diplomatic — allowed Lot to choose first to avoid conflict.
    - Obedient to God's command, patient and faithful.
    Strengths: calm, pleasant, and dependable; diplomatic and courteous; loyal and consistent worker; great listener and friend; easy to get along with and rarely offends; respects culture and order; a good teacher or team player who works steadily and faithfully.
    Weaknesses: passive and indecisive; often avoids responsibility or conflict; can be too compromising; slow and easily complacent; lacks motivation or initiative without encouragement; can be stubborn or resistant to change.
    Needs to learn: to become more proactive and decisive; to balance peacekeeping with assertiveness; to take initiative and finish tasks; to overcome fear of tension or confrontation.

    KEY TAKEAWAYS

    Melancholy — deep thinker, organized, dependable; main weakness: perfectionism and sensitivity; growth focus: accept imperfection.
    Choleric — decisive, visionary, hardworking; main weakness: pride and impatience; growth focus: practice gentleness.
    Sanguine — cheerful, social, inspiring; main weakness: disorganization and inconsistency; growth focus: develop discipline.
    Phlegmatic — calm, loyal, diplomatic; main weakness: passivity and indecision; growth focus: build initiative.

    Biblical and spiritual perspective
    Ellen G. White reminds us: "None can plead their temperament, their education, or their circumstances as an excuse for living in rebellion against God." (From the Heart, May 19)
    This means God expects growth from every believer, regardless of natural temperament. Through the Holy Spirit, our weaknesses can be transformed into strengths for His service.

    Conclusion
    Temperament shapes our behavior but does not define our destiny. Understanding our temperament helps us improve our relationships, serve more effectively in ministry, develop emotional maturity, and reflect Christ's character more clearly. Every temperament has a divine purpose — and when surrendered to the Holy Spirit, it becomes a powerful tool for leadership, service, and love.
    "The goal is not to change who we are but to let God refine who He created us to be."

    Evidence on file Big 5 Personality Traits.docx

    The OCEAN five-factor model, its history from Galton through Cattell and Costa & McCrae, and the limits of self-report.

    Read full document

    THE BIG 5 PERSONALITY TRAITS

    The Big Five personality traits are a psychological model consisting of five broad dimensions: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. Often remembered by the acronyms OCEAN or CANOE, these traits represent fundamental aspects of human personality and are considered to be consistent across different cultures and demographics.

    A brief description of each trait

    Openness — describes an individual's creativity, curiosity, and appreciation for new experiences and ideas.
    Conscientiousness — relates to an individual's organization, discipline, and tendency to be careful and diligent.
    Extraversion — encompasses qualities like sociability, assertiveness, and a tendency to seek out stimulation and social interaction.
    Agreeableness — involves being cooperative, kind, and trusting of others.
    Neuroticism — also known as Emotional Stability, describes the tendency to experience negative emotions like anxiety, anger, and sadness.

    According to this model, each person possesses varying degrees of these five traits, and their combination provides a comprehensive framework for understanding individual personality differences.

    • In psychology and psychometrics, the five-factor model (FFM) is the most common scientific model for measuring and describing human personality traits. The framework groups variation in personality into five separate factors, all measured on a continuous scale:
    • Openness (O) measures creativity, curiosity, and willingness to entertain new ideas.
    • Conscientiousness (C) measures self-control, diligence, and attention to detail.
    • Extraversion (E) measures boldness, energy, and social interactivity.
    • Agreeableness (A) measures kindness, helpfulness, and willingness to cooperate.
    • Neuroticism (N) measures depression, irritability, and moodiness.

    The five-factor model was developed using empirical research into the language people used to describe themselves, which found patterns and relationships between those words. For example, because someone described as "hard-working" is more likely to be described as "prepared" and less likely to be described as "messy," all three traits are grouped under conscientiousness. Using dimensionality reduction techniques, psychologists showed that most of the variance in human personality can be explained using only these five factors.

    Research into personality inventories found five broad dimensions could explain most variation in human personality and temperament, with more detailed analyses typically dividing the traits into more specific subfactors. For example, extraversion is typically associated with gregariousness, assertiveness, excitement-seeking, warmth, activity, and positive emotions. Other models, like HEXACO, supplement the Big Five with additional variables.

    The five-factor structure has been confirmed by many subsequent studies across cultures and languages, which replicated the original model and reported largely similar factors. The traits have predictive validity for objective metrics other than self-reports: conscientiousness predicts job performance and academic success, while neuroticism predicts self-harm and suicidal behavior.

    History of the Big Five
    The Big Five model originated from the lexical hypothesis, which suggests that the most important personality traits are encoded in language. Raymond Cattell built upon earlier lexical work by reducing thousands of descriptors to 16 personality factors, later clustered into five global traits, which some consider the "original Big Five." Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal then analyzed peer ratings of U.S. Air Force officers and derived five core dimensions: Surgency, Agreeableness, Dependability, Emotional Stability, and Culture — an approach later popularized by Warren Norman. In the 1980s, John M. Digman and colleagues consolidated evidence from previous studies and reaffirmed five major traits, while Paul Costa Jr. and Robert R. McCrae developed the NEO model, expanding it into the widely accepted Five Factor Model.

    Early history
    In 1884, British scientist Sir Francis Galton became the first person known to consider deriving a comprehensive taxonomy of human personality traits by sampling language — the idea known as the lexical hypothesis. William McDougall, writing in 1932, observed that "five distinguishable but separable factors" could be identified when looking at personality, suggesting "intellect, character, temperament, disposition and temper." In 1936, Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert implemented the lexical hypothesis, producing a list of 4,504 adjectives believed to describe observable and relatively permanent traits. In 1947, Hans Eysenck published Dimensions of Personality, positing that the two most important dimensions were "Extraversion" and "Neuroticism," a term he coined. In 1953, John W. French published an extensive meta-analysis of personality trait factor studies.

    Cattell's model
    In 1943, Raymond Cattell reduced Allport and Odbert's list to roughly 160 terms, added terms from 22 other psychological categories, and arrived at 171 traits. Through factor analysis he derived 60 "personality clusters or syndromes" plus seven minor clusters, narrowing this to 35 terms and later adding a 36th in the form of an IQ measure. In July 1949, Donald Fiske derived five factors: "Social Adaptability," "Emotional Control," "Conformity," "Inquiring Intellect," and "Confident Self-expression." That same year Cattell, with Maurice Tatsuoka and Herbert Eber, created the sixteen-factor 16PF Questionnaire. Its 4th edition (1968) identified five global factors: Extraversion, Independence, Anxiety, Self-control, and Tough-mindedness — which 16PF advocates have since called "the original big five." In 1978, Peter Saville determined the model could be reduced to five factors: Anxiety, Extraversion, Warmth, Imagination, and Conscientiousness.

    Tupes and Christal's model
    In 1957, Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal undertook a personality trait study of US Air Force officers, each rated by peers using Cattell's terms. In 1958 they analysed 37 personality factors from Cattell's, Fiske's, and Tupes' earlier work, deriving five factors labelled "Surgency," "Agreeableness," "Dependability," "Emotional Stability," and "Culture," further tested and explained in a 1961 paper. Warren Norman replicated their work in 1963, relabelling "Surgency" as "Extroversion or Surgency" and "Dependability" as "Conscientiousness," and finding four subordinate scales for each factor. Norman's colleague Lewis Goldberg continued this work.

    Limitations of self-report
    Much of the evidence on Big Five measures relies on self-report questionnaires, which makes self-report bias and falsification of responses difficult to account for. It has been argued that Big Five tests do not always create an accurate personality profile, since responses can be falsified — for example, by job applicants choosing answers that paint them in the best light. Research suggests a relative-scored Big Five measure, in which respondents make repeated choices between equally desirable descriptors, may be a potential alternative. When compared with a traditional measure for predicting GPA and creative achievement under both normal and "fake good" conditions, the relative-scored measure predicted these outcomes consistently under both, while the Likert questionnaire lost predictive ability under faking — proving less affected by biased responding.

Spiritual gifts — definitions from the curriculum manual

Read reference

SPIRITUAL GIFTS — FROM THE MASTER GUIDE CURRICULUM MANUAL

Every member of God's Church receives at least one spiritual gift from the Holy Spirit. A spiritual gift is a special ability given by the Holy Spirit to a member of the body of Christ that enables them to work with joy, effectively helping the church carry out its mission in the world. While everyone has different gifts, they work together through the divine power of the Holy Spirit, who chooses what gifts are given to each person.

Discovering spiritual gifts involves spiritual preparation through earnest prayer prompted by the Holy Spirit; asking daily for the baptism of the Holy Spirit; studying the Bible to learn and discern one's gifts as the Holy Spirit leads; and having an open heart and mind to submit to the Holy Spirit's guidance and confirmation from other church members.

Administration

The ability to organize, manage, and supervise, working with and through others to achieve goals. Its meaning is "to steer," as the helmsman or pilot of a ship.

Apostleship

To be sent out, especially commissioned to represent the church in a broader ministry. This gift may be represented today by the Spirit-given ability to begin work that leads to new churches being established.

Discernment

The analytical capacity to discern between truth and error, right and wrong.

Evangelism

The ability to so persuasively present the gospel of Jesus that people are led to become His disciples.

Exhortation

Derived from the same word Jesus used for the Comforter — one who comes alongside to encourage. Also the ability to stimulate people to action in the service of God.

Faith

The ability to see a vision of what God wants done and the unswerving confidence to accomplish it regardless of the obstacles.

Giving

The ability to share personal assets with joy and eagerness so that people are helped and God's work is advanced.

Helps

The ability to unselfishly meet the needs of others through practical help. The exercise of this gift often releases those with teaching and preaching gifts to minister the word of God.

Hospitality

The ability to open one's home graciously so that guests are put at ease and refreshed both physically and spiritually.

Intercession

The practice of praying earnestly and sincerely on behalf of others and their special needs.

Knowledge

The ability to easily master a body of truth, and to store and recall a fund of knowledge from God's Word to meet the need at hand.

Leadership

The ability to inspire and lead others in various ministries within the body of Christ. This gift is exercised with the attitude of a servant.

Mercy

The capacity to feel sympathy with those in need, especially those suffering, and to manifest this sympathy practically and cheerfully.

Missionary

The ability to minister across cultures.

Pastoring

The ability to shepherd, counsel, and encourage believers in their walk with Christ and in their service to church and community.

Prophecy

Primarily the gift bestowed on one called to receive divine revelation from God to be communicated to man; secondarily, the capacity to preach so that the Bible comes alive to the hearer.

Serving

The unusual desire and capacity to render service to others.

Teaching

The ability to instruct and explain Bible truths so clearly and in such detail that those willing to learn will understand.

Wisdom

The ability to penetrate into a matter, seeing the situation in its larger relationships, and imparting wise counsel from God's Word.

A caution from the manual

The devil always has a counterfeit for that which is genuine. Counterfeit gifts are often associated with the more visible — miracles, healings, speaking in tongues, and prophecy. Being more spectacular, they have greater power to catch attention. Manifestations of this order must be carefully tested by the church, for there will be miracles on both the side of truth and the side of error in the last days. Only by the Scriptures can they be tested.

The results of discovering your spiritual gifts include knowing God's will for your life and where you best fit into the work of the church; coping better with diversity and conflict in relationships; an improved sense of partnership with Jesus Christ as a result of being matched to the work most suited to you; and being better equipped to win friends and relatives to Jesus.

    Read full document

    CHRISTIAN STORY TELLING HONOR

    Christian Story Telling is the practice of using narratives to communicate Biblical truths, spiritual lessons and Christian faith.

    Name one source where you have found material for stories for each of the following categories. Tell a story from each category.

    1. Sacred history
    Stories in the sacred history category are Bible stories. These are obviously found in the Bible! However Bible stories are not always easy to tell to children as written in the Bible, so consider books such as My Bible Friends for a more storytelling friendly structure.

    Story of Daniel in the Lion's Den
    The story of Daniel in the Lion's den tells of his obedience to God. Daniel loved to talk to God daily and he did this publicly three times each day religiously. Some people in the King's palace did not like Daniel so they plotted to take his life by using his religious practices against him. These men tricked the King into passing a law that anyone found praying to another God except the King were to be cast into the den of lions. The King signed the decree and the men went to work to trap Daniel. Daniel did not change his routine but went ahead to his open window and prayed to God as he always did. When the men informed the King about Daniel's doings the King was very upset with himself but he could not take back his decree. He commanded that Daniel be cast into the lions' den telling him that his God will deliver him.

    The King spent the night fasting and was unable to sleep. Early the next morning he went to the lions' den and found that Daniel was still alive. Daniel told him that God had sent his angels to seal the lions' mouths shut and they had not hurt him. As a result of their actions the men who had plotted against Daniel along with their families were thrown into the den of lions and they were killed. Obedience to God by God's people will always result in the protection of His people.

    2. Church history
    These are the books that talk about the past of the church and how the church has been moving through the ages.
    Paul B. Ricchiuti has written several books covering church history at the Primary and Junior levels, including titles about Ellen White as friend of angels and trailblazer for God.

    3. Nature
    Jim Arnosky has written many excellent nature stories and field guides for the younger crowd. The life cycle stories of penguins, bees, ants, and frogs are truly fascinating, and children enjoy acting out life-cycle stories such as the penguin's journey to and from the sea, or the movements of the Sun, Earth, and Moon.

    4. Character story
    A character story is a story about a person — a famous person, a not-famous person, or someone you know — chosen to demonstrate good character (or, carefully, the consequences of poor choices).

    5. Object lesson with visual aids
    An object lesson warns of the outcomes that result from a particular behavior, as exemplified by figures such as Esau, Balaam's donkey, or King Saul, paired with a visual aid central to the story.

    Make a written outline of a story you are to tell.

    An outline is a hierarchical organization of an idea. The major bullets should include the setup (where, when, description of protagonist), the conflict (description of antagonist, nature of the conflict), the reaction to conflict (what antagonist and protagonist each do), and the resolution (how the conflict resolves and the aftermath).

    State how and under what circumstances course material is to be modified for the following

    Telling the story in first, second, and third person
    First person stories use "I", "me", "we" and "us" and are compelling because the audience knows they come from real experience. Second person stories use "you" and invite the audience to imagine themselves inside the story — well suited to Bible stories. Third person stories are about someone else; the audience may feel less personally engaged, but this form has its place, especially for well-known figures.

    Different audiences, ages, and purposes
    Young children need short stories that involve them physically and use vocabulary that matches their level. Older children can feel patronized by material that is too simple. A single story — such as Jonah — can be used to teach different lessons depending on which part is emphasized: obedience, God's inescapable call, love for other people, or simple wonder at creation.

Section II

Lifestyle Development (Stature)

Physical wellbeing, outdoor skill, and safety training that build a healthy, capable leader.

0%
Section summary

Lifestyle development

Stature is the physical dimension, and the manual makes a point that is easy to miss: lifestyle is not an isolated event but a lifetime process. The fitness requirement asks for a sustained three-month programme rather than a test you can pass in an afternoon. The honors that follow — water safety, camp safety, camping skills, temperance — are overwhelmingly about keeping other people alive and comfortable in the outdoors.

Temperance is the quiet centre of this section. The manual defines it as avoiding extremes of any kind, including excess in things that are good, and lists too much screen time, too much work, too much free time, and excessive fasting alongside the obvious vices.

What this section develops

  • That care of the body is stewardship rather than vanity, and that consistency matters more than intensity.
  • Risk assessment in outdoor settings — site selection, water, fire, food storage, and hygiene.
  • Practical competence: knots, navigation, cooking, shelter, and moving safely under difficult conditions.
  • That a current First Aid and CPR certificate is a standing obligation, not a one-time achievement.

    PHYSICAL FITNESS HONOR REQUIREMENTS AND NOTES

    Physical fitness is a state of health and well-being and, more specifically, the ability to perform aspects of sports, occupations, and daily activities. It is generally achieved through proper nutrition, moderate-to-vigorous exercise, and sufficient rest with a formal recovery plan. The five components of physical fitness are cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, and body composition. There are two kinds of physical fitness: health-related and sports-related. Examples of exercise include brisk walking, jogging, swimming, and biking. The three main types of physical activity are aerobic, muscle-strengthening, and bone-strengthening, with balance and flexibility work also beneficial; aerobic activity benefits the heart and lungs most.

    How to maintain fitness: think about your goals, make a balanced routine, start slow, build activity into your daily routine, include a variety of activities, try high-intensity interval training, allow time for recovery, and put your plan on paper.

    How to increase fitness: aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on two days a week.

    The difference between physical activity and exercise: exercise is a subcategory of physical activity that is planned, structured, repetitive, and purposefully focused on improving or maintaining one or more body parts.

    Benefits of physical activity include a better mood and reduced anxiety, better brain function and slower cognitive decline, lower healthcare costs, lower risk of heart disease and stroke, lower risk of type 2 diabetes, lower risk of several cancers, a longer life, stronger bones and muscles, fewer sick days, and — for children — better grades and classroom behavior. Regular activity can also make pregnancy and childbirth easier, aid weight control, and increase energy.

    A gym (from the Greek "gymnasion") is an indoor venue for exercise. The 3-3-3 gym rule refers to 3 days of strength training, 3 days of cardio, and 3 days of rest or active recovery. The 5-by-5 rule uses five exercises — squat, bench press, bent-over row, overhead press, and deadlift — in five sets of five reps. The "40% rule" holds that when the mind says quit, the body has typically used only 40% of its potential. "BF" refers to body fat percentage, averaging around 40% for women and 28% for men in most countries. The golden rule of fitness is goal setting, using SMART goals — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.

    Know how the following help to achieve a balance for your body

    • Exercise — improves heart and lung function and the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, helps control weight when balanced with diet, and produces mood-lifting endorphins. Our bodies were designed for regular activity, and exercise restores that natural need in an otherwise sedentary modern life.
    • Proper eating — a good diet supports physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual well-being. Calorie balance determines weight change regardless of starting weight; balanced vitamin, mineral, carbohydrate, protein, and fat intake keeps the body healthy, while imbalance (e.g., insufficient calcium) forces the body to draw on its own reserves, weakening bones, and excess fat contributes to heart strain.
    • Emotional stability — helps us positively handle stress; both exercise and diet affect it, with regular exercise serving as a healthy outlet for stress that also supports discipline in other areas of life.

    Define the following exercises

    • Isometric — muscles flex and hold a stationary position with no movement of a load; used often in physiotherapy and rehabilitation for its precise, adjustable intensity.
    • Isotonic — strength training performed against a specific opposing force where a body part moves against that force; the classic example is weightlifting.
    • Isokinetic — similar to isotonic, but resistance is applied through the entire motion, including the downward phase.
    • Anaerobic — requires very little oxygen uptake, such as sprinting, occurring in short bursts.
    • Aerobic — the most beneficial type, requiring sustained oxygen use over an extended period, such as jogging, swimming, or skating, improving cardiovascular health.

    Know the meaning of the principles involved in the following exercise program

    • Warm up — stretches and warms the muscles to reduce injury risk and gradually raises the heart rate.
    • Aerobic exercises — the main part of the program, raising oxygen intake and heart rate for at least 20 minutes.
    • Cool down — about five minutes of gradually slowing activity after the aerobic phase, protecting the heart from sudden strain.
    • Calisthenics — roughly ten minutes of strength-building work that reduces injury risk during future aerobic activity.

    Know how to determine your heart rate at rest and after exercise.

    Find your pulse at the wrist or over the heart; count beats over a 15-second interval and multiply by four (or 20 seconds ×3, or 30 seconds ×2), adding about 10% after exercise since the heart slows while you locate and count your pulse.

    Know how to determine the minimum rate at which your heart should be beating to obtain the best aerobic conditioning effect.
    For men: Rate = (205 − age/2) × 80%. For an 18-year-old man, half of 18 is 9; 205 − 9 = 196; 196 × 80% ≈ 157.
    For women: Rate = (220 − age) × 80%. For an 18-year-old woman, 220 − 18 = 202; 202 × 80% ≈ 162.

    Using the four steps above, complete a regular exercise program at least four times a week for three months, maintaining the minimum heart rate for at least 20 minutes each session, and keep a chart recording the type of warm-up, the aerobic exercise performed and its duration, and the calisthenics performed. Anyone over 35, or with a known health condition, should have a medical examination — including a stress test — before beginning. Warm up for two to three minutes with easy stretches, then choose an enjoyable aerobic activity such as cross-country skiing, swimming, running, jogging, skating, or cycling — anything that sustains the target heart rate for at least 20 minutes, not counting time before the target rate is reached; brisk walking works too, though it may take longer to reach the target.

  • Complete a three-month physical fitness program recommended by your doctor.

    BASIC WATER SAFETY HONOR (Personal and group research)

    How to enter and exit the water unassisted.

    The goal is to learn to get in and out of a pool without assistance and in a safe manner. To enter water unassisted, carefully approach the water's edge — the side of a pool or a stable shoreline — and, using a method like a sitting entry, lower yourself into the water while maintaining balance. Always enter unknown or shallow water cautiously, ideally feet first, to avoid unexpected hazards.

    Using the sitting entry method

    Position yourself — sit on the edge of the pool or a stable surface by the water.
    Place your feet — put your feet into the water, ensuring they are in a stable position.
    Support your body — place both hands on the pool edge to one side of your body.
    Turn and lower yourself — slowly turn your body and swing your legs under you while using your hands to lower yourself into the water.
    Maintain balance — keep your body touching the edge as you lower yourself to prevent falling.

    The best method to enter depends on the body of water and your surroundings. In most pools this can be done using a ladder, steps, ramp, or entering from the side. When using a ladder, it is important to enter and exit facing the ladder, which helps prevent slipping or falling off.

    Learn to put on a life jacket and float for thirty seconds.

    Life jackets need to be properly sized for the wearer, and children need a child life jacket. All buckles should be snapped into place and any ties securely fastened. The fit should be snug but not too constraining. In the water the jacket should stay put on the body, not float up above the wearer, which would make it useless and unsafe.

    How to call for help in case of an emergency.

    How you call for help depends on who needs help and where you are. If you are calling for someone else and have access to a telephone, dial the appropriate emergency number in your area. If you are calling for someone else and are in the water too, yell "Help!" as loud as you can; if a lifeguard is present, go to them as quickly as you can and tell them someone is in trouble. If you yourself need help while in the water, call out and wave your arms. Some lifejackets have a whistle, which is an excellent way to signal distress.

    Learn how to release a cramp.

    The most frequent muscle to cramp from swimming is the calf. To release a calf cramp while swimming, float on your back, stretch your legs out in front of you, and point your toes toward your head while pushing your heel away from your head, stretching the calf muscle. For muscles in the hamstring or buttocks, while back floating, use one hand to gently massage the tight muscle to release the cramp.

    Demonstrate reaching assist.

    Firmly brace yourself on a pool deck, pier, or shoreline by lunging down in a staggered stance (one foot forward, one foot back), shifting your center of gravity away from the water, and reach out to the person with any object that will extend your reach — a pole, oar, paddle, tree branch, shirt, belt, or towel. If no equipment is available, you can perform a reaching assist by lying down and extending your arm or leg for the person to grab.

    Learn at least ten safety rules when around water.

    Learn to swim before you go into the water. Make sure that you are safe to swim — free of currents and tides, during daylight, in safe water conditions, not overtired, and not immediately after eating, to avoid cramping or sickness. Swim near a lifeguard so help is available. Never swim alone; have at least one adult actively watching all swimmers. Supervise all children closely even when lifeguards are present, regardless of skill level. Don't rely on flotation devices such as rafts or floaties, as you may lose them in the water. Alcohol, drugs, and relaxing medications don't mix with swimming. Protect your head, neck, and spine by never jumping or diving into unfamiliar waters, and never go headfirst into shallow water (less than 9 feet or 3 meters). As soon as you believe you may be in trouble, call or wave for help. Follow all facility regulations and lifeguard directions. Swim parallel to shore if you wish to swim long distances. Stay hydrated — you do not feel sweat while in the water and can easily become dehydrated, leading to heat exhaustion. Protect your skin with SPF 30 or higher against harmful UV rays that can lead to skin cancer over time, reapplying every 90 minutes if in the water.

    CAMPING SKILLS 1

    Understand and practice wilderness and camping etiquette, regarding preservation of the outdoors.

    Review and practice the Leave No Trace 7 Principles: plan ahead and prepare; travel and camp on durable surfaces; dispose of waste properly; leave what you find; minimize campfire impacts; respect wildlife; be considerate of other visitors.

    Be considerate of other campers — choose tent colors that blend with the environment at frequented campgrounds, though bright colors help you find an isolated tent again, and wearing bright colors such as orange is important where hunting is allowed. Keep noise down, camp out of sight of trails where guidelines require it, never cut through another camper's site, and leave every area cleaner than you found it.

    Know eight things to do when lost.

    Don't panic — take a breath and relax. Pray. Look around for something recognizable, such as a trail blaze. Listen for sounds of other campers, traffic, or water. If nothing is recognizable, stay put. If you have a map and compass, try to locate your position using hills, valleys, or streams. If you try to relocate the trail, mark your starting point clearly and circle outward in widening loops while keeping the marker in sight; if that fails, stay where you are. Use a whistle or shout in patterns of three, the universal call for help, and repeat every 15 minutes. Do not climb a tree or steep hillside. If it's near sunset, prepare a shelter and a fire, and stay put through the night.

    Be familiar with various types of sleeping equipment suitable to location and season.

    Rectangular sleeping bags are common and roomy but provide the least warmth for the most weight, with no hood to retain heat. Mummy bags are shaped to the body, tapering at the feet and head with a drawstring hood, wasting very little space or warmth. Barrel bags are a roomier, heavier version of the mummy bag.

    Know fire safety precautions.

    Keep a clear 10-foot radius around the fire; never light beneath overhanging branches, tents, or shelters; avoid accelerants; extinguish fires completely before leaving (cool enough to touch); never build directly on flammable ground cover; keep water, sand, or an extinguisher nearby; never remove burning sticks; watch for stray embers; wear proper footwear; and never light a fire in high winds, drought, or where prohibited.

    List personal items needed for a weekend campout.

    Warm-weather clothing: thick socks, jeans, light shirts, a wide-brimmed hat, and boots. Cold-weather clothing, layered: thermal underwear, synthetic shirts, a wool sweater, windbreaker, fleece or snow pants, overcoat, wool socks, boots, and a warm hat (wool holds warmth even wet; cotton does not). Sleepwear for comfort and modesty. Personal gear: sleeping bag, ground pad, flashlight, pocket knife, toilet paper, coins for showers, Bible and devotional material, camera, notepad, toiletries, towel, and a mess kit.

    CAMPING SKILLS 2 (Personal and group research)

    Develop a personal philosophy of outdoor etiquette, such as courtesy to other campers and outdoor conservation.

    Review and practice the Leave No Trace 7 Principles, and be considerate of other campers — using muted tent colors at busy campgrounds, bright colors like orange where hunting occurs, keeping noise down, never cutting through another site, and leaving every site cleaner than you found it.

    Know and understand the six W's for the selection of a good campsite: Wind (camp where you're shielded, judging direction from leaning trees), Water (fresh water nearby but away from flooding or mosquito-heavy marshes), Weather (know local patterns), Wild things (watch for large mammals and small hazards like snakes and ticks), Wood (enough for a fire, with no dead branches overhead), and Willingness (permission from the landowner and proper permits).

    Demonstrate your ability to protect the wilderness and your water source by proper personal hygiene and cooking sanitation.
    Use established toilet facilities where available; otherwise dig a cat hole (about 10 cm deep) or a latrine for larger groups, at least 60 meters from any water source. Wipe dishes clean, wash in soapy water, rinse in a second tub with a little bleach, and dispose of grey water at least 60 meters from water.

    Know how to safely light and use a camp stove and lantern.

    Connect the canister properly, light the lighter near the burner first, then turn on the gas — never the reverse, to avoid a dangerous flame flare.

    Know safety rules and demonstrate your ability to properly cut firewood; demonstrate how to break dead wood properly.
    Prop the log on a support with the cut point beyond the support so the saw doesn't pinch; smaller dead wood (up to about 7 cm) can be broken underfoot near a support instead of sawn.

    Explain two ways to keep camp food cool.

    Store food in a cooler with block ice, which lasts longer than cubes; or place food in a waterproof, mesh-wrapped container secured in a stream, or wrap it in wet burlap and hang it so evaporation cools it, re-wetting occasionally.

    Demonstrate tent site selection; properly pitch and strike a tent; describe precautions for a wet tent; properly clean, dry, and store a tent.
    Choose flat ground away from ridge tops (wind, lightning) and dry stream beds (flash floods), above the high-water line near rivers, and on the lee side of a hill. Check overhead for falling hazards. When pitching, lay out the ground cloth and canopy, stake the door location, insert poles before raising them together, then add the fly. When striking, wait for morning dew to evaporate if possible; inspect and sweep the interior, stow the fly inside the canopy, then remove poles (pushing rather than pulling sectional poles) and fold the tent. Never store a tent wet — dry it fully first to avoid mold and mildew.

    Show proper ways to stuff or roll your sleeping bag or bed roll for travel, and describe how to properly clean it.

    Use a stuff sack if provided; otherwise zip the bag, fold it lengthwise along the tie-strings, roll tightly from the opposite end, and tie off. To clean, turn it inside out, hang it, and beat out dust; air it fully; avoid machine washing unless the label specifically allows it.

    Note: the tent color for Camping Skills #2 patch is red — Blue/Friend/Camping Skills I, Red/Companion/Camping Skills II, Green/Explorer/Camping Skills III, Silver/Ranger/Camping Skills IV.

TEMPERANCE HONOR — WHAT YOU MUST DO

Skill level 2 · General Conference · Sourced from the AY Honors requirement listing.

1. Memorise and sign the Temperance Pledge — a promise, with God's help, to live a Christian life of true temperance in all good things and total abstinence from tobacco, alcohol, and other narcotics.

2. Memorise two Bible texts and two Ellen G. White quotations, chosen from these lists.

Bible texts

  • Romans 12:1, 2
  • 1 Corinthians 10:31
  • 1 Corinthians 6:19, 20
  • Proverbs 20:1
  • Galatians 5:22, 23
  • 3 John 2

Ellen G. White

  • Temperance, p. 3
  • Counsels on Diet and Foods, p. 428
  • Temperance, p. 201
  • Temperance, p. 113
  • The Ministry of Healing, pp. 327-328

3. Do four of the following

Write and deliver a speech of five to eight minutes.
Write an essay of 150-200 words on alcohol, tobacco, drugs, or physical fitness, setting out your own commitment to a healthy lifestyle.
Write a four-line jingle on a drug prevention topic.
Draw or make a poster, roughly 22 by 28 inches, on the harmful effects of a drug, tobacco, or alcohol.
Make a substance abuse exhibit for a local shopping centre, library, or school.
Make a scrapbook of at least 20 pages showing drug prevention advertising.

4. Share what you accomplished with at least five people outside your immediate family, and collect their signed Temperance Pledges.

5. Discuss and role-play what you would do if: a close friend offers you a cigarette; a classmate offers you money to sell marijuana; an older relative offers you a beer; a stranger's cigarette smoke is bothering you; a friend asks you to smoke marijuana; or you are at a gathering with a friend who gets drunk and insists on driving you home.

Note: the essay and the speech are your own work and your own convictions — that is the point of the honor. Your Nutrition honor notes give you solid material on the physical effects to draw from.

    BASIC RESCUE HONOR — REQUIREMENTS AND NOTES

    What is the definition of an emergency rescue?

    A rescue is the act of removing someone from danger. An emergency rescue is a technical term for a rescue taking place under hazardous circumstances and with high risk to the rescue personnel, but which must be done immediately to save a person's life. In this type of scenario, if the victim is not removed from their circumstance as quickly as possible they will die quite soon. Technical rescues describe many types of circumstances — in all cases the victim is in danger, though a cat up a tree or an uninjured person stuck in a crashed car is not likely to die in moments but will still need someone with the means and skill to help.

    Basic rescue involves following key principles to ensure the safety of both the rescuer and the victim, with the primary goal of getting the injured person out of immediate danger and to medical help as quickly as possible.

    Core principles of basic rescue
    Safety first — your own personal safety is paramount. Never put yourself in a situation where you become a second victim. Always assess the scene for potential dangers and use appropriate personal protective equipment.
    Assessment — quickly evaluate the situation and the victim's condition. Identify hazards (live wires, smoke, unstable structures) and determine the required urgency and resources.
    Communication — establish clear communication with other rescuers and keep the victim informed about what is happening.
    Prioritization (triage) — if there are multiple casualties, prioritize rescues based on the severity of injuries and who is in the most immediate danger.
    Action plan — develop a plan of action based on the assessment, and choose the safest possible rescue method.
    Aftercare — once the victim is out of immediate danger, provide basic first aid until medical help arrives.

    Triage in first aid: prioritizing care
    Triage is the process of assessing and prioritizing injured or ill individuals based on the severity of their condition, ensuring the most critical cases receive immediate attention while others receive care in order of urgency.
    Principles of triage: Immediate care (red tag) — life-threatening injuries requiring urgent attention. Delayed care (yellow tag) — serious but non-life-threatening injuries. Minor care (green tag) — mild injuries that can wait for treatment. Expectant care (black tag) — critical cases unlikely to survive even with medical intervention.
    Triage steps: 1. Assess the scene, ensuring safety before approaching victims. 2. Check for responsiveness to identify unconscious or severely injured individuals. 3. Evaluate breathing and circulation; if a person is not breathing, start CPR. 4. Control bleeding, stopping heavy bleeding first to prevent shock. 5. Move or mark patients, labelling them for medical responders in large emergencies.

    Show how to safely rescue a person from the following situations

    1. Being in contact with a live electric wire.

    First, do not touch a person who is in contact with a live electric wire — the electricity will also flow through your body, and there will be two victims instead of one. If you can quickly turn off the power source, do so immediately. If it cannot be turned off quickly, try to knock the wire away with something that does not conduct electricity, such as a shoe (taken off first), a wooden broom handle, or a wooden chair. Once the victim has been separated from the power source, check for breathing, and if the victim is not breathing, begin artificial respiration.

    2. A room filled with smoke.

    In a fire, a person is far more likely to die from smoke inhalation than from exposure to flames. Remember two things about smoke: it rises, and if you inhale enough of it, it will kill you. If you find yourself in a smoke-filled room, get down and crawl. If you can, cover your mouth and nose with a wet cloth to filter the smoke; if water is not available, a dry cloth is better than nothing. Make your way to the door, and if it is closed, feel it — if it is hot, do not open it, as this means there is fire on the other side. Find another way out, such as a window or another exit.

    3. Clothes on fire.

    Get the person to the ground and roll them over and over. Another option is to wrap the victim with a blanket, coat, or jacket if one is handy. If your own clothes catch fire — stop, drop, and roll.

    4. Drowning, using a non-swimming rescue.

    Unless you have been trained to do so, avoid swimming to the assistance of a drowning person. A drowning non-swimmer is typically in a panic and may grab onto anyone or anything within reach to keep their airway above the surface; if the victim submerges the rescuer, the rescuer's life is endangered and the original victim has nobody to assist them. Instead of entering the water: talk the victim in, coaching them to kick their legs; throw a life ring, life jacket, or other flotation device; reach an item such as a rope, pole, oar, or paddle to the victim and pull them in once they grab it; wade into shallow water and attempt the above; or row out in a boat and try the above from within the boat.

    Show ways of attracting and communicating with rescue aircraft.

    • Make a distress signal on the ground by piling rocks, branches, or other debris to form large letters spelling "S.O.S." — the universally recognized signal for help. Use materials that contrast with the surrounding environment; in winter you may be able to stomp an SOS into snow. Make the letters read east to west so the shadows catch them better.
    • Light three fires, built either in a line or a triangle, and get them good and hot. When you see a rescue plane during daylight hours, add green plant matter to the flames to create thick smoke, being careful not to extinguish the fire.
    • Use a signaling mirror. The emergency signaling mirror is approximately 3 by 5 inches, consisting of an aluminized reflecting glass mirror, a back cover glass, and a sighting device. It attracts the attention of passing aircraft or ships by reflection, in sunlight or hazy weather, and can be seen at a distance of 30 miles at an altitude of 10,000 feet. To use it: punch a cross-hole in its center; hold the mirror about 3 inches in front of your face and sight through the cross at the ship or aircraft; while keeping sight of the target, adjust the mirror until the spot of light on your face disappears into the hole — the bright spot will then be aimed directly at the search ship or aircraft.

    Indications for the need of an immediate rescue.

    1. The victim has stopped breathing. 2. The victim has severe bleeding. 3. The victim is being electrically shocked. 4. The victim has had a heart attack. 5. The victim is on fire. 6. The victim is drowning. 7. The victim has been poisoned.

    Procedures to follow before moving a victim from a life-threatening situation.

    The first task is to assess the whole situation and plan the rescue. Be sure you can perform the rescue without injuring yourself. Make sure that moving the victim will not cause additional injury. Know where you intend to move the victim before lifting them. If bystanders must be used, brief them in thorough detail on what you want them to do. Unless the danger is immediate, any first aid should be given before moving the victim. If you suspect a spinal injury, do not move the victim.

    Principles involved in moving a victim from a life-threatening situation.

    Be sure that it is necessary to move the victim; if it is not, do not move them. Know how you will move the victim before trying. Know where you will move them before trying. Be sure you are able to lift the victim before lifting; if too heavy, drag them instead. Maintain your balance, and do not start the move from an unbalanced position. Keep your footing throughout the move.

    Proper ways to help a victim without assistance — one-rescuer methods.

    • Never move the casualty any further than you have to. Scan the escape routes to determine the best method and route to carry the casualty. If you're alone and must move the casualty quickly, try one of the following:
    • Human crutch — only for casualties who can help themselves; an easy way to move the less seriously injured.
    • Drag carry — used to drag a casualty lying on their back or in a sitting position. Ease your hands under the casualty's shoulders and grasp the clothing on each side, supporting the head between your forearms, and drag backward only as far as necessary for their safety, being careful not to choke them when pulling on their clothing.
    • Blanket drag — an alternate method, using a blanket to support and pull the casualty.
    • Pick-a-back — lift the casualty from a standing or sitting position onto your back; don't try it if the casualty is unconscious or has arm injuries.
    • Firefighter's crawl — use a triangular bandage or torn shirt to tie the casualty's hands together and place them around your neck, allowing you to move a person much heavier than yourself.
    • Fireman's carry — if there are no indications of injury to the spine or an extremity and the victim cannot walk. Place the casualty in a supine position; lie down on your side along their uninjured or less injured side, your shoulder next to their armpit; pull their far leg over your own, holding it there if necessary; grasp their far arm at the wrist and bring it over your upper shoulder as you roll and pull the casualty onto your back.

    The six W's of campsite choice, fire safety, three fire lays, tool sharpening, and latrine building.

    Read full document

    CAMPING SKILLS 3

    Review six points in the selection of a good campsite (Wind, Water, Weather, Wild things, Wood, Willingness), and review the safety rules of fire building.

    The six W's: Wind (find a wind-protected area, judging direction from leaning trees); Water (fresh water available, but away from flooding and mosquito-heavy marshes); Weather (know local patterns); Wild things (watch for large mammals and small hazards); Wood (adequate wood, no dead wood overhead, check trees for wind risk); Willingness (permission and permits secured).

    Fire safety rules: keep a 10-foot clearance; never light beneath overhanging branches, tents, or shelters; avoid accelerants; extinguish completely before leaving; never build on flammable ground cover; clear the sod first and keep it moist to replace later; keep extinguishing supplies handy; never remove burning sticks; watch for stray embers; wear proper footwear; and never light a fire in adverse conditions or where prohibited.

    Lay the following three fires and tell their uses

    • Hunter's Fire — a cooking fire with logs spaced closely enough to support a pot, pan, or Dutch oven, laid as level as possible; the same type of fire used for open-flame roasting.
    • Reflector Fire — either a log or rock reflector, placed opposite the fire so the item to be baked (or the camper, for warmth) sits between the fire and the reflector, which throws heat back.
    • Star Fire — logs arranged in a star pattern meeting at a central flame; as the ends burn they are pushed inward, avoiding the need to cut logs to length.

    Know how to properly sharpen a hatchet and knife.

    Use a whetstone rather than a power grinder, which can overheat and untemper the steel. For a hatchet, pass a file over the edge at a steep angle on each side. For a knife, hold the blade at about a 15-degree angle and draw it along the whetstone, sharpening both sides.

    Properly locate and build a latrine, and describe its importance to the individual and the environment.

    Consider water flow and your water source when choosing a location — never place a latrine within 60 meters of any water supply, and be considerate of other campers downstream. A latrine has two parts: an enclosure for privacy (tarps, a teepee frame, or an old tent shell) and a commode built over a dug hole, with dirt and a shovel kept nearby to bury waste gradually and control smell; fully bury the hole when breaking camp.

    Note: the tent color for Camping Skills #3 is green — Blue/Friend/Camping Skills I, Red/Companion/Camping Skills II, Green/Explorer/Camping Skills III, Silver/Ranger/Camping Skills IV.

    CAMPING SKILLS 4

    In Camping Skills 4, the tent colour is silver, symbolizing the fourth class in Pathfinder club, the Ranger class.

    Preservation of the wilderness: discussing etiquette and conservation.

    Review and practice the Leave No Trace 7 Principles: plan ahead and prepare; travel and camp on durable surfaces; dispose of waste properly; leave what you find; minimize campfire impacts; respect wildlife; be considerate of other visitors. Choose tent colors that blend in at busy campgrounds, or bright colors in isolated areas or where hunting is allowed; keep noise down; never cut through another camp; and leave every site cleaner than you found it, even turning cleanup into a friendly contest with younger campers.

    How to start a fire in wet weather, knowing where to get tinder and how to keep your fire going.

    Split open a log to find dry wood at its center for both kindling and fuel; once the fire is lit, lay wet logs nearby to dry, turning them to dry all sides.

    Know the wood best suited for making a quick, hot fire.

    Conifer wood (pine, fir, spruce) is full of flammable sap and burns hot and fast, ideal for starting a fire, though it leaves no good bed of coals.

    Know the wood best suited for making coals for cooking.

    Hardwoods, especially hickory, mesquite, and oak, leave a good, long-lasting bed of coals.

    Demonstrate how to split firewood.

    Get a firm footing, ensure the axe head is secure and the blade sharp, clear the swing path of obstacles, keep hands dry, ensure no one is in the swing radius, and rest before you become too tired to swing safely.

    Demonstrate the proper care and storage of camp foods and how to build various caches to protect food from animals.

    Never store food in a sleeping tent. If a vehicle is available, seal food tightly inside it. Otherwise, suspend food at least 3 meters above the ground and well clear of the trunk and branch it hangs from, since bears can climb.

    Purify water by four different methods.

    • Boiling for five to ten minutes.
    • Iodine, added as solution, crystals, or tablets, which kills most common pathogens.
    • Chlorine — two drops of 5% bleach per liter, left covered for 30–60 minutes.
    • Filtering, using small, portable water filters.
