    DRILLING AND MARCHING HONOR (Personal and group research)

    Explain five or more objectives of drilling.

    Order — helps maintain an organized unit. Morale — training discipline and group unity. Enjoyment — a fun activity that promotes use of imagination. Fellowship — helps one learn to take and give orders. Leadership — builds confidence in giving orders. Self-control — attention to the leader. Respect — regard for the rights of others.

    Define the following

    Formation — the arrangement of Pathfinder drill elements in a prescribed manner. Line — elements side by side, abreast of each other. Rank — a line one element deep. Interval — the distance between people standing next to each other. Column — people standing one behind another. File — a single column. Distance — the space between people within a column, front to back. Cover — aligning yourself with the person in front while maintaining correct distance, shown by raising the left arm at a 90-degree angle, not shoulder level. Flank — the right or left side of a formation, from within it. Cadence — the uniform rhythm, or steps per minute, at which a movement is executed.

    Explain the actions in each of the following groups

    At Ease, Stand At Ease, and Parade Rest — Parade Rest is the strictest of the three, called only from Attention: feet about 8 inches apart, hands in the small of the back, right over left, eyes forward. Stand At Ease is slightly more relaxed, with eyes following the commander. At Ease allows movement (except the right foot, which stays planted) but requires silence and standing. Rest is even more relaxed and permits talking, with the right foot still planted.

    Mark Time, Quick Time, and Double Time — Mark Time means marching in place while maintaining interval and distance. Quick Time is marching at 120 steps per minute with roughly a 24-inch step, arms swinging naturally. Double Time is 180 steps per minute at the same step length, initiated with forearms raised horizontally.

    Hand Salute and Present Arms — Present, Arms is a one-count salute given at Attention: the right hand's fingers touch the eyebrow (or glasses rim, or cap brim), upper arm parallel to the ground, no bending at the joints. Order, Arms lowers the arm smartly without a slapping sound. Hand Salute is the same movement given without a command, used when reporting or showing courtesy, with the head turned toward the person addressed.

    Right (Left) Flank and Column Right (Left) — commands to turn a marching unit in the indicated direction, executed on the matching foot strike, with the leading marcher pivoting and the rest of the unit following in sequence while maintaining alignment.

    Properly execute the following basic movements: Attention (feet together at a 45-degree angle, hands curled at the sides, eyes forward, silent); Parade Rest; Stand At Ease; At Ease; Dress Right Dress (extending the left arm and turning the head right to align with the file to the right, until "Ready Front" is called); Prayer Attention (like Parade Rest, but with bowed heads and headgear removed by male members); Present Arms; Order Arms; Right Face and Left Face (pivoting on the heel and toes to turn 90 degrees); About Face (turning 180 degrees using the right foot behind the left heel); and Fall Out (breaking formation without leaving the area, distinct from Dismissed).

    Properly execute the following movements: Mark Time (marching in place, correcting intervals); Forward March (stepping off with the left foot, left foot on the "odd" beat in 4/4 time); Rear March (stepping with the left foot, pivoting 180 degrees on the toes, then stepping off again with the left foot); and Halt (called on the left foot, with a final half-step bringing the feet together at Attention).

    NUTRITION HONOR

    Nutrition is the process of eating and absorbing food that your body needs for nourishment. It involves breaking down food into nutrients. Nutrients are chemical substances your body needs to function.

    Explain why a high fiber diet is important and tell how this can be obtained.

    Fiber promotes the wavelike contractions that keep food moving through the intestine. High-fiber foods expand the inside walls of the colon, easing the passage of waste. Fibrous substances pass through the intestine undigested and absorb many times their weight in water, resulting in softer, bulkier stools. Insoluble fiber is found in wheat, rye, bran, and other grains, and in most vegetables.

    Name three diseases due to malnutrition and describe the symptoms of each.

    • Scurvy — results from insufficient vitamin C and leads to livid skin spots, spongy gums, and bleeding from mucous membranes, most abundant on the thighs and legs; the person looks pale, feels depressed, and is partially immobilized. It was once common among sailors and soldiers separated from fresh produce for long periods.
    • Beriberi — a nervous system ailment from vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, with symptoms including weight loss, emotional disturbance, impaired sensory perception, weakness and pain in the limbs, irregular heartbeat, and tissue swelling; in advanced cases it can cause heart failure and death. It occurs in people whose staple diet is polished white rice, and can pass to infants through a thiamine-deficient mother's milk.
    • Rickets — most commonly caused by vitamin D deficiency, which prevents calcium absorption, leading to fragile or malformed bones, bone pain, slowed growth, dental problems, muscle loss, and increased fracture risk.
    • Pellagra — a niacin and tryptophan deficiency disease with symptoms of red skin lesions, diarrhea, dermatitis, weakness, mental confusion, and eventual dementia; common among those whose diet relies heavily on corn.

    What are the symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency?

    Unusual fatigue, faulty digestion, no appetite, nausea, loss of menstruation, numbness and tingling of hands and feet, nervousness, diarrhea, and mild depression. Since B12 cannot be obtained from plant sources, vegans are advised to eat fortified foods or take supplements.

    What is the difference between saturated and unsaturated fats? Which is most healthful and why?

    Saturated fats and trans fats are most likely to cause heart disease. Saturated fats are found mainly in animal products and in coconut, palm, and palm kernel oil; trans fats appear in hydrogenated foods like margarine and crackers. Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats — canola, olive, flaxseed oil, nuts, avocado, soy, and nut butters — reduces heart disease risk.

    Why is it advisable to use less sugar in our diet? Suggest several ways this may be accomplished.

    Excess sugar is linked to a suppressed immune system, cancer risk, heart disease, appendicitis, multiple sclerosis, raised cholesterol and blood pressure, drowsiness in children, Alzheimer's disease, and liver tumors. Ways to cut back include reducing gradually, going half and half, setting rules about dessert, eating sweets with meals rather than alone, choosing better breakfast cereals, not skipping meals, not adding sugar to food, and substituting a walk for a sugar craving.

Section III

Spiritual Growth (Favor with God)

Deepening a personal walk with Christ and grounding it in Scripture, devotion, and heritage.

0%
Section summary

Spiritual growth

This is the longest section on the card, and the manual explicitly encourages you to run several of its requirements at once: the Gospels, the devotional journal, and the 28 Fundamental Beliefs can all be worked through in the same daily devotional hour. Read that as guidance about pace — this section is built around a sustained habit rather than a series of tasks.

The progression is deliberate. You study Christ in the Gospels, keep a record of what God is teaching you, work through salvation in Steps to Christ, articulate all 28 beliefs in your own words, then teach five of them to others. Understanding is proved by the ability to explain it to someone else.

What this section develops

  • Christ as the model for leadership — personal, patient, and invested in a small number of people.
  • That personal devotion is irreplaceable, and that writing it down lets you see growth you would otherwise miss.
  • Why Adventists hold what they hold, well enough to give a reason for the hope you have (1 Peter 3:15).
  • The sanctuary and Christ’s ongoing ministry, and the pioneer history that shaped the movement you serve.

    Evidence on file Desire of Ages Summary.docx

    Reflection on Christ's life and ministry — His compassion, humility, and the plan of salvation.

    Read full document

    DESIRE OF AGES

    The Desire of Ages by Ellen G. White is a devotional book that explores the life of Jesus Christ. The book tells the story of Jesus' life, from His birth to His death and resurrection. It highlights Jesus' teachings, miracles, and interactions with people, showcasing His love and compassion. Through Jesus' life, it illustrates the love of God and the plan of salvation.

    It highlights His interactions with various individuals and groups, including the Samaritans and the sick at Bethesda. It emphasizes the cultural tensions between Jews and Samaritans, illustrated by Jesus' encounter with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, where He breaks social norms by asking her for water. It also details Jesus' healing of a long-term cripple at the pool of Bethesda, showcasing His compassion and authority.

    The book emphasizes Jesus' role as the Messiah, who came to save humanity from sin. It highlights His humility, kindness, and selflessness, setting an example for us to follow.

    Throughout the book, emphasis is made on the importance of faith, trust, and obedience to God. It encourages us to develop a personal relationship with Jesus, who can satisfy the deepest longings of the human heart. The book shows the love of God, demonstrated through Jesus' sacrifice on the cross.

    In conclusion, the Desire of Ages is the love of God, demonstrated through Jesus' life, teachings, and sacrifice. The book invites us to come to Jesus, learn from Him, and follow His example of love and service. By exploring Jesus' life, we can gain a deeper understanding of God's love and plan for our lives. This devotional classic has inspired millions of people and remains a valuable resource for spiritual growth and reflection.

Curriculum manual · reference

How to build the written requirements — a working structure

Read reference

HOW TO BUILD THE WRITTEN REQUIREMENTS

These requirements cannot be filled in from a reference book — the Conference reviewer is assessing your understanding and your walk, not a summary of someone else's. What follows is a working structure for each, so you can sit down and write.

The devotional journal — one month minimum

Set a fixed time and keep the entries short and honest; a paragraph a day is enough. For each entry note the passage you read, one thing you understood that you had not seen before, and one thing you intend to do differently. Every week or so, write a slightly longer entry answering how your faith has moved in the last seven days. The manual explicitly allows you to read the Gospels, The Desire of Ages, and the 28 Fundamental Beliefs during this month, which means one disciplined month can carry four separate requirements at once.

The Education reflection — one page

Open with what you expected the book to be about and what it actually turned out to argue. Then take two or three specific ideas — Ellen White's treatment of the teacher's influence, of nature as a classroom, of character over information — and for each, say plainly how it changes something you do in your club. Close with the single change you are making first. Specific beats broad every time.

The Steps to Christ reflection and two Share options

Log the chapters as you go; the reviewer wants the daily record. For the Share options, the easiest honest pair is presenting a devotional to your club drawn from one chapter, and discussing three concepts from the book with a group. Keep your devotional notes and record the group's names and date.

The 28 Fundamental Beliefs — one paragraph each

Use the same three-part shape for all 28 so the work stays manageable. First, state the belief in your own words in one or two sentences. Second, give the key verse or verses it rests on. Third, write one sentence on what it means for how you live or lead. Three or four a day finishes the set inside a fortnight, and the manual notes these paragraphs then become the basis for the five lessons you teach.

The spiritual gifts and personalities reflections — two pages each

Take the survey first, then write. Cover the gifts the survey identified in you, whether you recognise them from experience, which gifts you see in the leaders around you, how knowing this changes how you assign work in your club, and where your own weaknesses mean you need others. The personalities paper follows the same pattern using your temperament or Big Five result.

A practical note

Write these in your own voice, including the parts where you are unsure. A reviewer reading twenty portfolios can tell the difference between a candidate who wrestled with a book and one who summarised it, and the honest version is always the stronger one.

THE 28 FUNDAMENTAL BELIEFS — GUIDANCE FROM THE MANUAL

As a future Master Guide, it is important that you have a firm understanding of the beliefs of the Seventh-day Adventist Church. Your role as a youth leader will give you many opportunities to share, clarify, and teach these topics. The requirement to prepare a one-paragraph personal reflection on each belief is critical to your ability to provide accurate answers.

Just as important as memorization is an understanding of the concepts presented. We are called "to be thinkers, and not mere reflectors of other people's thought." This is why we need to fully understand why we believe what we believe, and "always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have." (1 Peter 3:15)

Seventh-day Adventists accept the Bible as the only source of our beliefs, holding to the Protestant conviction Sola Scriptura — the Bible as the only standard of faith and practice for Christians.

The 28 beliefs organise into six categories

  • The Doctrine of God
  • The Doctrine of Man
  • The Doctrine of Salvation
  • The Doctrine of the Church
  • The Doctrine of the Christian Life
  • The Doctrine of Last Day Events

In each teaching, God is the Architect who, in wisdom, grace and infinite love, is restoring a relationship with humanity that will last for eternity.

What your paragraphs must contain

Include the key verse or verses connected to each Fundamental Belief in every paragraph.
Reflect on how the belief informs your walk with God, so that you have a ready answer for those who inquire about your faith.
Even though this requirement seems simple at first sight, summarising an entire Fundamental Belief requires a thorough knowledge of the subject.

    SANCTUARY HONOR REQUIREMENTS AND NOTES

    The three main parts of the sanctuary and the courtyard.

    The three main parts of the sanctuary and courtyard were the Court, the Holy Place, and the Most Holy Place.

    The Court: The Altar of Sacrifice (acacia wood overlaid with bronze), the Laver (bronze).
    Holy Place: Table of Showbread (acacia wood overlaid with gold), Seven-branched Golden Lampstand, Altar of Incense (acacia wood overlaid with gold).
    Most Holy Place: Ark of the Covenant with the Mercy Seat and covering Cherubim (made of gold) — Aaron's rod (which budded and bore fruit), stone tablets with the Ten Commandments, and a gold bowl with manna were placed in the ark (Hebrews 9:4).

    Tell what each piece of furniture represents.

    Altar of Sacrifice: Jesus's sacrifice. Laver: cleansing from sin, a form of baptism. Table of Showbread: Jesus, the Bread of Life. Seven-branched Lampstand: Jesus, the Light of the world (oil = the Holy Spirit). Altar of Incense: prayers ascending to Heaven, the intercession and merits of Christ. Ark of the Covenant: the presence of God (Ten Commandments). Mercy Seat: the meeting place. Cherubim: God's attributes.

    How many coverings were over the sanctuary?

    Four layers: an inner royal liner of red, blue, and purple linens; bleached white goat's hair; ram's skin dyed red; and badger's skin (also translated durable leather, fine leather, seal's skin, or goatskin), plain and brown.

    Tell what each covering represented.

    The inner royal liner represents Jesus — red for Christ's life, blue for His obedience, purple for royalty, gold for purity. The woven goat's hair represents Jesus's perfection and purity. The ram's skin dyed red represents the blood of Jesus. The badger's skin represents Jesus covering His divinity with humanity.

    The following colors were used in the sanctuary and in the priests' clothing. Tell what each color represented.
    Red: Christ's blood (Hebrews 9:11–12). Blue: obedience (Numbers 15:38–39). Purple: royalty (Mark 15:16–18). White: righteousness, purity (Revelation 19:8). Black: sin (1 John 1:5). Gold: divinity in Heaven (Job 22:25). Silver: longing desire — the Hebrew word for yearn shares a root with the word for silver. Brass: divinity on Earth (Philippians 2:5–8 — fully God and fully man).

    What kinds of animals were brought daily to the courtyard?

    A young bull, rams, heifers, lambs, goats, and pigeons or doves — all ceremonially clean, without spot or blemish (John 1:29).

    Describe the robe of the common priest.

    Linen breeches as an undergarment, woven of one piece, spotless and without blemish; a plain white linen robe and turban; sandals removed before entering the Sanctuary (Exodus 28 and 39).

    Describe the robe of the High Priest.

    Like all priests, linen breeches as an undergarment, then an embroidered linen coat tied with an embroidered girdle, and over that a one-piece sleeveless solid blue robe with golden bells and pomegranates on its hem. Over the blue robe went the ephod — gold, blue, purple, and scarlet fine twined linen, fastened at the shoulders with two onyx stones engraved with the names of the tribes of Israel. On the ephod sat the breastplate, holding the Urim and Thummim next to the High Priest's heart, through which God made known His will, and on its outside twelve precious stones arranged in four rows of three. He wore a mitre on his head, with a gold plate inscribed 'HOLINESS TO THE LORD' fastened to the front with a blue ribbon (Exodus 28 and 39).

    Evidence on file 2300-Day Prophecy.docx

    Explanation of Daniel 8:14, the year-day principle, and the 1844 investigative judgment.

    Read full document

    2300-DAY PROPHECY

    With the aid of an illustration or diagram, explain the 2300-day prophecy.

    This prophecy is described in Daniel 8, where Daniel has a vision of a ram, a goat, and a little horn. He is told in Daniel 8:14, "For two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed."

    Time period: the 2300 days are understood to represent 2300 years, based on the day-for-a-year principle in prophecy (Ezekiel 4:6; Numbers 14:34).

    Sanctuary cleansed: the cleansing of the sanctuary is interpreted as divine judgment and the purification of God's people, connected in Christian theology to Christ's return and the final judgment.

    Prophecy key events

    • Ram and Goat — the ram represents the Medo-Persian empire, the goat represents Greece; the little horn is often interpreted as a power that would defile the sanctuary in the period following Greco-Roman influence.
    • Cleansing of the Sanctuary — associated with the Day of Atonement in Jewish tradition, symbolizing the work of Christ in the heavenly sanctuary, bringing an end to sin and restoring purity.

    Outline of the 2300-day prophecy

    • Start of the prophecy (Persian Empire time).
    • The rise of the Greek Empire (Hellenistic period), with the division of the empire.
    • The Little Horn, symbolizing the papal power or other forces that defiled the sanctuary — a period of control over religious practice.
    • 2300 years, beginning in 457 B.C. (the decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem).
    • End of the 2300 years, 1844 A.D. — for Seventh-day Adventists, the beginning of Christ's heavenly judgment.

    Breakdown: 457 B.C. (decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem) to 1844 A.D. (cleansing of the sanctuary/judgment) spans the full 2300 years.

    Seventh-day Adventist perspective on the 1844 A.D. interpretation

    Seventh-day Adventists believe the 2300 years ended in 1844 A.D., marking the beginning of the "investigative judgment" in the heavenly sanctuary — the start of Christ's final work before His second coming, judging the living and the dead.

    Conclusively, the 2300-day prophecy, from the decree to rebuild Jerusalem in 457 B.C. to 1844 A.D., is interpreted as marking a period of purification and judgment in the heavenly sanctuary, focused on divine intervention and the ultimate restoration of God's people.

    Evidence on file Sanctuary & Heritage Summary.docx

    The great controversy from Eden through the sanctuary and judgment, tracing Scripture's unfolding storyline.

    Read full document

    SANCTUARY AND HERITAGE SUMMARY

    The church starts in Eden with Adam and Eve, then Abel and Cain — though other children born to them are not named in the Bible, as they are not central to the salvation story.

    The great controversy is kick-started in Genesis 3:15. When the Lord removed Adam and Eve from the Garden of Eden, three forms of conflict were declared: there will be enmity between the woman (the church) and the snake; between the seed of the woman (believers) and the seed of the snake; and the woman's seed — singled out as Jesus Christ — will crush the snake's head while the snake strikes His heel.

    The devil has fought this battle with two main weapons: persecution and amalgamation.

    Persecution is first witnessed when Cain kills Abel. God gives Adam and Eve another son, Seth, who Genesis 5:3 says resembled Adam — introducing the "sons of God" of Genesis 6:1–7, while Cain's line became the "sons of men." Cain showed he was not on God's side by presenting produce from cursed land instead of a lamb — missing the point that a lamb pointed to Christ's coming sacrifice, which is why his offering was rejected.

    Amalgamation appears in Genesis 6:1–7 when the sons of God intermarried with the sons of men, and Satan successfully mingled evil people with God's people. By Noah's time witchcraft was rampant and people had lost the way of God. God gave that generation 120 years, but they still refused to believe, showing that God gives every generation a grace period before He lets them go. The flood came from water commanded from the firmament and beneath the earth, not ordinary rain, washing away the defiant. Being part of God's visible church does not guarantee salvation — only those who trust and believe are kept.

    After the flood, Satan initiated the building of the Tower of Babel near the site of Eden, the same area where Babylon was later built by Belshazzar (Babylon comes from Babel). In Ezekiel 8, Satan is described as recreating his own trinity: Nimrod as the father, Thames as the son, and Thelamis (Nimrod's wife) as the holy spirit — a counterfeit designed to obscure the knowledge of the true God.

    In Genesis 12, God calls Abraham while he had no knowledge of God, since Satan had by then largely dissolved information about Him. God promised Abraham blessings and a nation, requiring him to walk by faith, while Satan brought a drought to push Abraham's family toward Egypt, where Hagar entered the picture. Hagar, said to be a trained sorcerer, tapped into Abraham's fear of dying without the promised son, leading to the birth of Ishmael and other sons who became nations. When Abraham realized his mistake he sent the other sons away and kept Isaac, the promised son, in Canaan. Hagar and Ishmael later returned to Egypt to strengthen sorcery there. Moses wrote the book of Genesis roughly 2000 years after these events.

    Satan mainly attacks family and the Sabbath because the Sabbath concerns who is worshipped — the same issue behind Lucifer's fall — and family is where the church nurtures its next generation, so Satan targets it early, before a fighting faith can develop. Isaac faced the same witchcraft problem as his father, but God worked through Joseph to secure a safe future for His people. Families such as Laban, Esau, Ketrah, and Rebecca remained in Canaan, Mesopotamia, Sodom, and Gomorrah, blindfolded by witchcraft around them.

    Genesis 15:12 prophesies that Abraham's descendants would be displaced for 400 years before returning to Canaan. In Exodus 14, as Moses led Israel back toward Canaan, Satan tried to sabotage the journey through Pharaoh's army, and later in the wilderness, so that only the younger generation who had not seen Egypt — apart from Caleb and Joshua — crossed into Canaan after 40 years. God's church then expanded from a family basis to a nation ruled first by judges, beginning with Joshua, though the nation's faith remained weak.

    After Joshua's death (Joshua 24:29), leadership shifted to kings, starting with Saul (chosen by the people) and David (chosen by God), continuing through to King Hezekiah's era, when Israel was eventually conquered by Nebuchadnezzar's Babylonian army beginning in 605 B.C. Though Jeremiah prophesied a 70-year captivity, Daniel realized only part of that time had passed and prayed on Israel's behalf; an angel told him the prayer had already been answered but was delayed by the "prince of Persia."

    Many prophets spoke of the Messiah's coming, but Daniel gives the exact timeline, and Jesus was born around 3 B.C. John the Baptist later announced that the kingdom of Heaven was at hand, reflecting a time of confusion as the Jews, weary of Roman rule, awaited a Messiah they expected to appear as a conquering king rather than the humble figure Jesus became. From 3 B.C. to A.D. 27, Jesus did little in public, following the tradition that a man reached full ministry standing at 30; His baptism, marked by the Spirit descending as a dove and a voice from heaven, was meant to be a turning point of belief, though many still failed to recognize Him because they expected glory rather than humility.

    Revelation 12:1 summarizes the entire salvation story through its symbols: the woman is the church; the sun is Christ, revealed through the New Testament; the moon is the lesser light — the Old Testament — pointing to the New; the twelve stars are the sons of Jacob who founded Israel; the male child is Christ, whom Satan tried and failed to destroy; the dragon is Satan; the wilderness is a place of restriction and despair; the 1260 days represent the 42 months or three-and-a-half prophetic years; the tail represents lies; and a third of the stars represent the fallen angels.

    Recommended reading: Patriarchs and Prophets, Prophets and Kings, The Desire of Ages, Christ's Object Lessons, Acts of the Apostles, and The Great Controversy — five (six) books tracing this same storyline from Eden to the end of the great controversy.

Fundamental Belief #24 — Christ's Ministry in the Heavenly Sanctuary

Read reference

FUNDAMENTAL BELIEF #24 — CHRIST'S MINISTRY IN THE HEAVENLY SANCTUARY

There is a sanctuary in heaven, the true tabernacle made not by human hands. There Christ ministers on our behalf, making available to believers the benefits of His atoning sacrifice offered once for all on the cross. Jesus' ultimate sacrifice gives us confidence to approach God, knowing we are forgiven. Now Jesus is reviewing our lives before returning to take us home, so there is no question that His judgments are made in love.

At His ascension, He was inaugurated as our great High Priest and began His intercessory ministry, which was typified by the work of the high priest in the holy place of the earthly sanctuary. In 1844, at the end of the prophetic period of 2300 days, He entered the second and last phase of His atoning ministry, which was typified by the work of the high priest in the most holy place of the earthly sanctuary.

It is a work of investigative judgment which is part of the ultimate disposition of all sin, typified by the cleansing of the ancient Hebrew sanctuary on the Day of Atonement. In that typical service the sanctuary was cleansed with the blood of animal sacrifices, but the heavenly things are purified with the perfect sacrifice of the blood of Jesus.

The investigative judgment reveals to heavenly intelligences who among the dead are asleep in Christ and therefore, in Him, are deemed worthy to have part in the first resurrection. It also makes manifest who among the living are abiding in Christ, keeping the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus, and in Him, therefore, are ready for translation into His everlasting kingdom. This judgment vindicates the justice of God in saving those who believe in Jesus. It declares that those who have remained loyal to God shall receive the kingdom. The completion of this ministry of Christ will mark the close of human probation before the Second Advent.

Scriptural basis

Leviticus 16; Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6; Daniel 7:9-27; 8:13, 14; 9:24-27; Hebrews 1:3; 2:16, 17; 4:14-16; 8:1-5; 9:11-28; 10:19-22; Revelation 8:3-5; 11:19; 14:6, 7; 20:12; 14:12; 22:11, 12.

    The Bachwanga name, Nchwanga mission, and the pioneers who planted Adventism in Uganda from 1927 onward.

    CHURCH HERITAGE

    A brief background of Nchwanga, the Home of the Seventh-day Adventists.

    In Uganda, Seventh-Day Adventists are affectionately known as the "Bachwanga." This nickname has its roots in the country's rich history, specifically in the conflicts between the Bunyoro-Kitara and Buganda kingdoms during the pre-colonial and early colonial periods.

    Before the arrival of colonialists, the Bunyoro kingdom, under Omukama Kamurasi, had achieved a level of prosperity that surpassed its neighbouring kingdoms, including Toro and Buganda. With the succession of Omukama Kabarega and the influence of colonial powers, the Buganda kingdom began to gain strength and expand its territories, leading to civil wars between the two kingdoms fought with bows and arrows.

    Local legends recount fierce battles at a place called Bwanswa, in Bugangayizi County, formerly part of Buganda but lost to Bunyoro. Fighters hid in rocks and caves to launch attacks, and many arrows missed their targets and broke upon hitting the rocks — leading the Banyoro to rename the area Nchwanga, meaning "the breaking of arrows" (from "Nchwe," meaning breaking, and "Nga," the wild reeds used for arrows).

    With the arrival of colonialists, Nchwanga was settled as a buffer zone between the Banyoro and Baganda. Two European settlers were given land to plant coffee and rubber. In the early 1920s the land was gazetted for sale, catching the attention of the Adventist mission. Spencer Maxwell was sent to purchase it, marking the establishment of the first Adventist mission station in Uganda, and the name Nchwanga became synonymous with Adventists in Uganda — hence "Bachwanga."

    The Early Days of Seventh-day Adventism in Uganda
    The idea of establishing the church in Uganda was first conceived in South Africa in March 1903. In June 1903 Brother Booth visited Uganda to assess the situation and found many people eager to learn, with authorities offering favourable terms for a mission station. Despite this early enthusiasm, the work did not officially begin until 1927 — 24 years later — likely due to political and religious unrest and disease-carrying insects in the region.

    The first Seventh-day Adventist to enter Uganda was E.C. Enns, a German missionary from Tanzania, in 1906, though he could not stay long. Between 1924 and 1926, pioneer volunteers Spencer George Maxwell and W.T. Bartlet were appointed. Maxwell led a group of six volunteers, including three couples from Tanganyika, and after being unable to secure land from the Kabaka of Buganda, they were directed to Nchwanga, where land had been advertised for sale. Maxwell secured the land, and by the end of 1926 he and Petero Kime Risase had organised Nchwanga as a mission office. Maxwell also wrote Christian books to help spread the gospel. 1927 is officially considered the starting point of the Adventist message in Uganda.

    The Advent of Adventism in Buganda
    Maxwell and his friends were redirected to Mityana district, Busimbi Subcounty, Bwanswa village, where a native named Ananias Guggwa welcomed them and offered a small grass-thatched kitchen as a base. Petero Risase, Msangi, and Rewe lived there and spent their days visiting natives, returning late to prepare meals at night — earning the village the name Bulyakiro ("eating at night"). Today the village is known as Kiyudaya, from "Bayudaya" (Jews), due to the Adventists' observance of the Sabbath.

    According to local legend, when Kabaka Chwa II of Buganda visited Mityana, Risase paid him a courtesy call, and the Kabaka donated land for a church — now the SDA Church Mityana site at Kiyudaya, Busimbi. Books such as The Great Controversy and Patriarchs and Prophets were distributed, though it took nearly two years to gain converts. The first was an old blind man, Joshua Kiddawalime, baptized at Nchwanga.

    Risase and Rewe continued door-to-door evangelism, winning converts including Simon Golola, Henry C. Guweddeko, and Blandina Namusoke, an Anglican family baptized at River Mpamuguju. Simon Golola and Henry became strong evangelists, starting a Sabbath school at Kalamba. In Mityana, Hajji Mulindwa became the first Muslim convert to Adventism.

    In 1934, Missionary Volunteers secured land at Kireka Hill, with Risase playing a central role, while Andersen established the Kakoro mission in eastern Uganda. Kireka became a base from which Adventism spread to Ndese, Najjanankumbi, Kayunga, Bugerere, Seeta-Nazigo, Makerere, and Kikajjo. By 1941, SDA Kireka Primary School had three classes. The growth of Adventism in the region was closely tied to families — once converted, believers often donated land and helped build churches, as seen with the Parmas family in Najjanankumbi.

    Leaders of the Seventh-day Adventist Church Uganda Union

    Spencer G. Maxwell (1927–1928), G.A. Illingworth (1929), V.E. Toppenberg (1930–1943), G.A. Lewis (1944–1947), R.D. Wieland (1948–1953), M.E. Lind (1954–1955), F.H. Muderspach (1956–1958), W.B. Robinson (1959), M.E. Lind (1960), I.E. Schultz (1961–1962), D.K. Bazara (1963–1968), R.D. Plfer (1970–1971), D.B. Wheeler (1972), R. Cater (1972/1973), D. Isabirye (1973–1980), S.B. Kyambadde (1981–1982).

    After reorganisation in 1983: Central Uganda Field Mission — President S.B. Kyambadde (1983–1988); Western Uganda Field Mission — C.M. Aliddeki (1983–1988).

    Uganda Union Mission after reorganisation in 1989: Bohannan Jack (1989–1990), S.B. Kyambadde (1991–1995), C.M. Aliddeki (1996–2000), J.L. Wani (2001–2009), John Kakembo (2009–2014), Daniel Matte (2015–2022), Maka Moses Ndimukika (2023–2025), and Pr. Samuel Kajoba (present).

    Key points to note

    • Nchwanga Mission office was established in 1927 by S.G. Maxwell.
    • Kireka Hill established by Petero Risase in 1932 and 1934.
    • Kakoro mission office established by Andersen in 1932.
    • Katikamu Wobulenzi mission office established by Muderspach in 1943.

    Biographical study of Ellen G. White as part of a pioneer-personalities series for this honor.

    Ellen G. White

    Ellen Gould Harmon was born on November 26th, 1827, in Maine, U.S.A., and died on July 16th, 1915 (aged 87). Ellen Harmon grew up in Portland, Maine, where her father was a hat maker. At the age of nine, a stone thrown by a schoolmate smashed Ellen's face, damaging her nose. The injury was serious, limiting her to a third-grade education. Ellen found comfort in her faith and joined the Millerite movement at a later age; she was 17 years old by the time of the Great Disappointment, and wrote, "We were disappointed, but not disheartened." Her husband was James White, and together they had four children.

    She was an author and co-founder of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, writing many books to strengthen believers in their faith, including Steps to Christ, The Desire of Ages, Education, and others. She received a vision of comfort after the Great Disappointment in December 1844, seeing that Christ is still leading His people to the heavenly city — that though the journey is long, those who keep their eyes on Jesus will reach the heavenly city safely.

Section IV

Community Development (Favor with Man)

Turning faith outward through evangelism, fellowship, and service to others.

0%
Section summary

Community development

Favor with man is the outward-facing section, and the manual keeps widening the circle: from personal evangelism, to honors that equip you to cross cultural and social divides, to fellowship inside your own congregation, to service alongside people who may not share your faith at all.

Two cautions in the manual are worth carrying. First, evangelism is defined broadly — sharing a testimony, feeding the homeless, and holding public meetings all count. Second, when working with outside organisations you are told to respect their rules, including any policy on proselytizing, because sometimes your life and your service are the better sermon.

What this section develops

  • That evangelism is a process and a relationship rather than an isolated event.
  • How to build bridges across cultures the way Jesus did, and how to de-escalate conflict biblically.
  • That the local church is a fellowship community, not only a Sabbath morning service.
  • That service given without conditions attached is itself a witness.

    Evidence on file Cultural Diversity Appreciation — Honor Work.docx

    Research on culture, stereotyping, and unity across cultural lines, grounded in Scripture (1 Cor. 9, Eph. 2, Gal. 3).

    Read full document

    CULTURAL DIVERSITY APPRECIATION HONOR — SUMMARY AND GROUP RESEARCH WORK

    This honor is one of the oldest honors, introduced in the early 1960s. Its objectives are to develop an awareness and appreciation for the cultural diversities within our church, society, and community at large.

    Define Culture.

    Culture is the arts, customs, and habits that characterize a particular society or nation — the beliefs, values, behavior, and material objects that constitute a people's way of life. While a group's art is often considered the mark of culture, it is actually the daily habits of a group of people that primarily mark their culture as different from another's.

    Cultural diversity.

    Cultural diversity is the variety of human societies or cultures in a specific region, or in the world as a whole — for example, in Austria, Uganda, and New Zealand. Uganda's own cultural diversity includes the Baganda, Banyankole, Banyarwanda, Batooro, Bakiga, Bakonjo, Barundi, Bachooli, Badaama, and Banyoro, among many other groups. Christianity itself modifies culture, so a Christian group differs in culture from the group it came from.

    Different cultures coming together is referred to as cultural diversity. As Master Guides, we should respect other people's cultures and unite for the gospel, per the Great Commission — God created us in different cultures so we might build each other up and become one body in Christ. Nothing can be accomplished while divided by cultural wrangling, which is why Jesus, before returning to heaven, told His disciples to remain together in the upper room and wait for the Holy Spirit — promoting unity across their different personalities and backgrounds so they would be ready to spread the gospel.

    Among the disciples were the talkative, the short-tempered, the silent, the peacemakers, the prayerful, tax collectors like Matthew, and zealots like Simon — yet all became united in spirit, and the early church grew steadily as a result. There is a secret in being united, and Master Guides should always emphasize unity within the church, society, and community.

    "United we stand, divided we fall." As Master Guides, we should always ensure and emphasize unity amongst our church, society, and community at large.

    1 Corinthians 9:20 shows that Paul, though raised in Rome, adapted his conduct and lifestyle to spread the gospel with ease. Reaching people of a different culture requires understanding that culture; adopting some of its practices — as Paul did — helps people feel accepted and builds trust, so long as the practice doesn't conflict with the Adventist faith. Where a cultural practice cannot be reconciled with the faith, missionaries develop an alternative — for example, a home-blessing ceremony that invites God into a new house instead of a ceremony involving witchcraft. Christianity should fit within every culture, changing hearts rather than turning everyone into typical Westerners.

    Ephesians 2:14 addresses the barriers and disunity that had developed in the Ephesian church between people of different cultures and lifestyles — originally between Jews and Gentiles, but applicable to any two cultures today. Christians should accept and love other Christians as Christ does.

    When this honor was first written, a Pathfinder generally had to look across an ocean to study another culture. Today, in much of the world, the world's cultures have come to us, and traditional minorities are, collectively, increasingly becoming the majority in many regions. What can you do to reach across cultural divides and build friendships that incorporate cultural diversity?

    Christians should also accept and love non-Christians from every culture, because this is the only way people will meet Jesus as their Savior. Greater appreciation of cultural differences would make the world safer, happier, and less violent — more like Heaven.

    Galatians 3:27 — "For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ" — indicates that all believers are equal in Christ's eyes; being "clothed in Christ" means a believer's sins are covered regardless of their culture, and no one is any better than another. A Christian Jew worshipping in Jewish style, a First Nations church following native practices, and an African tribesman who prefers storytelling through song are all equally valid in God's eyes; a person does not need to live far away to be in a different culture, and visiting an Adventist church rooted in a different culture from one's own can show how we all share the same faith while expressing it differently.

    Despite our cultural differences, let us hold the Bible as our standard of measurement, while reaching people in a good way, because we are all sinners saved by grace. All people belong to different cultures, with different lifestyles, languages, and ways of living, and we should appreciate them as they are.

    Note: task yourself as a Master Guide to research your local church members — their cultures, how they behave, how they talk, and how they carry out tasks, more so within their own churches. This helps us live in harmony and unity with our fellow church members, an essential gospel principle.

    Define stereotype and identify how you may have stereotyped people in the past.

    A stereotype is a conventional, formulaic, and oversimplified conception, opinion, or image — a person regarded as embodying a set image or type. Stereotyping means judging a person based on what we think we know about their "type" (because of race, sex, religion, etc.), sometimes subconsciously — for example, a sudden feeling of fear upon seeing a person of a different race in a lonely place, or assuming a woman must enjoy baking or sewing rather than repairing a car.

  • Peacemaker
  • Social Media
    Evidence on file Social Media Honor.docx

    Types of social media, their advantages, dangers and pitfalls, and using an online profile to reflect Christian character.

    Read full document

    SOCIAL MEDIA HONOR (Personal and group research)

    What is social media?

    Social media is the means by which communication among user groups is encouraged by creating, sharing, and exchanging information of interest. Social media differs from traditional media (newspapers, television, magazines, radio, outdoor displays) in many ways, but most significantly by who controls the message and content. Social media is democratized, with anyone with internet access able to join, generate content, promote content, and discuss content, whereas traditional media is controlled by a corporation and its staff who decide what messages are sent out and what feedback is shared.

    Define the following types of social media, giving a current example of each.

    • Internet forum — a web-based dialogue site that promotes discussion through short messages, facilitating organized threaded conversations. Forums often retain posts for a long time and may be searchable. PHPBB is a popular, free-to-use forum package, and many hobbies have large forums devoted to the topic.
    • Text messaging — the process of sending short messages among two or more devices over a network. This form of media has now developed into sending pictures, video, and sound.
    • Social network service — designed to connect people who share common interests through the internet. Each person has a profile listing their interests and information they choose to reveal about themselves. Facebook is perhaps the largest example.
    • Social blogs — a site designed for discussion or information purposes containing post messages. These sites allow comments along with images, and give bloggers the opportunity to build social relations with their readers.
    • Podcast — a digital audio file made available on the internet for downloading to a computer or mobile device, typically available as a series whose new installments subscribers receive automatically. Podcasts take many forms, including sermons, seminars, blog-like presentations, opinion pieces, and serial programs similar to a radio show.
    • Social bookmarking — the process of tagging and sharing references to resources found on the internet. Users can share, edit, and annotate web documents; the main information is not saved, just a bookmarked link and perhaps brief explanatory text. Reddit is an example, though this is an ever-changing area, and some bookmarking sites focus on photos or video.

    What are some advantages, disadvantages, and pitfalls one should be aware of when using social media?

    Advantages
    Social media is fully capable of bringing people together from all backgrounds due to a common interest. It is an excellent tool for marketing and promotion. You can find things, people, and resources very quickly. It can be used as a medium to learn from others, reading what people are thinking about topics of interest. Information can be spread very quickly. Large-scale protests and entire revolutions have been organized via social media. It is relatively hard for repressive governments to control, giving people freedom of expression in ways not previously possible.

    Disadvantages
    Posting negative information can have a serious impact. Used the wrong way, social media has a tendency to drive people away from what could be a very informative discussion. Using it for selling without engaging customers face to face, or without responding to negative feedback, can have considerable repercussions to your reputation. Incorrect, damaging, and even dangerous information can spread quickly — for example, a viral campaign encouraging battered women to mark their palm as a distress signal was dangerous precisely because abusers, not professionals, were the ones who saw the sign. Computer viruses and malware links are shared over social media. Child predators use social media to lure children; thieves may spot when your family is out of town from vacation photos; identity thieves can guess passwords and security answers from your profile. Terrorists use social media to recruit.

    Pitfalls
    There are serious issues of privacy to consider, and one should be careful about what private information is released for the world to see and act upon. Some business owners set their expectations too high when using social media to advertise. Cyberbullying can cause considerable damage to victims. Inappropriate social media use can cause people to lose jobs, fail in a run for public office, lose relationships, and face other real-world consequences. Posting slander can have legal consequences as well as personal damage to reputation.

    Discuss with a group the importance of maintaining your integrity when posting information about yourself and responding to posted information about others, including ethics, personal safety, and parental accountability.
    It is important for Pathfinders to understand the times we live in, where information posted through social networks remains the property of the social network provider. Information posted — no matter how complimentary or derogatory it may seem — remains available for others to view, and for anyone reading your post, their first impressions of your character may become validated in their mind. This is why social media should be used as a tool to represent the character of Christ.

    Pathfinders must understand that their online profile is a significant representation of them as individuals. It defines who they are and the values they represent, as well as what they prefer others to think of them. This may not necessarily reflect who they actually are, but it will leave a lasting impression on those who view their profile. Positive information should be shared — information that presents their character in a positive light — since anyone from a potential employer to a church member can freely look at their profile to acquire an idea of the "real" person they are dealing with. The same rules apply to responding to posts: be mindful of language or slang that does not reflect the person you want others to see.

    Discuss with a group how social media can be used to engage different types of learners.

    Visual — learn by physical demonstration, pictures, and words that stir up the imagination.
    Auditory — learn mainly by listening.
    Read/Write — learn by reading material and writing information.
    Kinesthetic — learn through hands-on experience and active participation.

Share Section & Investiture

Evidence gathered for the portfolio review, and what is required to be invested as a Master Guide.

0%
Section summary

Sharing and investiture

The Share Section is not a requirement in its own right — it is the mechanism by which several other requirements are demonstrated. Each time the card says "do two Share Section options," you choose from these six and file the evidence. The same option may be reused for different books and topics.

The manual’s reasoning is that knowledge kept to yourself is treasure hoarded, and that both extroverts and introverts can find a form of sharing that suits them. Investiture then closes the programme: a church board that knows you recommends you, a Master Guide verifies your portfolio, and you receive the scarf, slide, pin and patch.

What this section develops

  • That teaching something is the test of whether you have understood it.
  • How to document what you share so that it stands as evidence: names, dates, links, scripts, audiences.
  • That the local church has a real say in who leads its youth, and that this is a safeguard rather than an obstacle.
  • That a portfolio review returns Complete or Incomplete, and an Incomplete is a correction with a route back.
